CHAPTER-III
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES OF THE MINISTRY
Rehabilitation of J&K Migrants and Security related Expenditure (SRE)
8.0       The targeted attacks by the militants against civilians in the initial phases of the terrorist violence in J&K forced
a large number of Kashmiri Pandits and a sizeable number of Sikhs and other Hindus and a few Muslims-to migrate
from the Valley in 1990s. There were 56487 migrant families as per official records. The Central Government initiated a
policy to provide relief and rehabilitation to such families/people. The thrust of the policy was to minimise the
difficulties and hardships of the migrants and provide a reasonable amount of sustenance and support. Various State
Governments/UT Administrations were reimbursed by the Central Government for providing relief to such Migrants.
8.1.0    On being asked about the reasons for shortfall in the performance of the scheme of rehabilitation of J&K
Migrants and a saving of Rs. 184 crore, the Ministry clarified that the provision of funds were made under “Security
Related Expenditure” and “Relief and Rehabilitation” for J&K for the financial year 2004-05 taking into consideration
the expenditure incurred during the preceding year, as well as the anticipated expenditure during the year. The Ministry
also informed that a Committee was set up to look into the condition of the migrants who were till now living in one
room tenements. It was further stated that since the families living in relief camps have grown and one room tenement is
highly inadequate for them for proper living there is need for at least two room tenements. The Ministry informed that it
has started making efforts to convert one-room tenements into two rooms by merging two tenements.
8.1.1    The Ministry has furnished the details of the BE & RE, final expenditure, savings for SRE and Relief and
Rehabilitation as follows:—

8.1.2    Following reasons have been attributed by the Ministry for the savings under SRE and Relief and Rehabilitation
for the State of J&K:—
            (i)         Surrender of a provision of Rs. 40 crore which was earmarked for Parliamentary Elections 2004. As the
elections were held ahead of schedule, expenditure was met from the budgetary allotment of 2003-04;
            (ii)        Items like arms, ammunitions, vehicles, security and communication equipments, security works
previously funded under SRE were transferred to Police Modernisation Schemes during the financial year 2004-05.
Accordingly, a provision of Rs. 60 crore under SRE was transferred to Police Modernisation Scheme by re-
appropriation for release to the Government of Jammu and Kashmir;
            (iii)       SRE schemes are operated on a reimbursement basis. Because of heavy snowfall and avalanches in the
State, the State Government has claimed less amount of reimbursement;
            (iv)       The reasons for saving under Relief and Rehabilitation inter-alia include less expenditure on surrender
of militants under the new policy than anticipated, slow pace of the construction of 200 flats at Budgam for
rehabilitation of Kashmiri migrants and difficulties faced in the utilization of funds earmarked for shifting of villages on
LoC; and

for preferring the claims promptly, thereby adding further increase in savings.
8.2       Replying to a query about commencement of the scheme for the rehabilitation of J&K Migrants and quantum of
expenditure spent so far, the Ministry has informed that Relief to Kashmiri Migrants is being provided since the
migration started in 1990. Till 2003-04, an expenditure of Rs.653.85 crore has been incurred on tents, cash assistance,
free ration, civic amenities, construction of one-room tenements, improvement of infrastructure and grant for
camps/schools. The expenditure was reimbursed under ‘Security Related Expenditure’. During the current financial
year, an amount of Rs. 35.74 crore has been reimbursed as ‘Assistance to Kashmiri Migrants’. In addition, an amount of
Rs. 6.60 crore was provided under PM’s Special Package in 1996 for construction of one-room tenements for migrants.
The Committee was also informed that a study team of Advisor, Planning Commission and Joint Secretary in Ministry
of Home Affairs had studied the living conditions of migrant camps. The team had found living conditions grossly
inadequate.
8.3       The Committee expresses its deep concern over the living conditions in rehabilitation camps of Kashmiri
migrants in Jammu and Delhi and Government’s dilemma and lack of clear vision on the future of these migrants. The
Committee is of the considered view that the migrants should be sent back to the valley only when adequate security of
their lives and properties is ensured. Keeping in view the living conditions in the camps, the Committee feels that
Government instead of projecting a saving Rs. 174 crore under Relief and Rehabilitation, should have utilised the full
amount allocated under the said head for improving the living condition in these camps. The Committee is also of the
view that instead of conducting studies on migrants some concrete steps to improve their living conditions should be
taken urgently.
Police strengthening on Indo-Nepal Border
9.0       The stretch of 1751 Kms. of Indo-Nepal border covering 5 States and 20 districts is now being guarded by the
Shasastra Seema Bal (SSB). Its charter of duty was amended on the recommendation of the Group of Ministers under
the policy of ‘One border One force’. Earlier the Indo-Nepal border was guarded by BSF and ITBP. Besides that, the
respective State Police also take care of the security aspects in the area for which the Ministry of Home Affairs has a
special scheme of reimbursement of expenditure on Police infrastructure and intelligence network.
9.1       On being asked about the reasons for shortfall in the ‘Police strengthening on Indo-Nepal border’ the Ministry
has stated that pursuant to the acceptance of recommendations of Group of Ministers on Reforming the National
Security System by Government of India, the State Governments having border with Nepal were asked to send proposal
for strengthening of policing infrastructure and intelligence network in their respective areas. A provision of Rs.21 crore
was kept in the BE 2004-2005 for reimbursing the expenditure to be incurred by the respective State Governments on
police strengthening and intelligence network etc.
9.2       The Ministry further stated that while reviewing the scheme it was found that there was a lot of overlapping
between the proposed scheme and the scheme of Modernization of Police Forces (MPF). The MPF scheme also
provides for similar assistance to the State Governments for modernizing their police forces. It was, therefore, felt that it
would be administratively prudent to link this scheme with the existing scheme of Modernization of Police Forces by
providing a special component under the MPF scheme for giving assistance to the States having border with Nepal to
strengthen their policing and intelligence network. Due to this change in policy necessitated by administrative and
financial propriety, the funds kept for this purpose in BE 2004-2005 could not be utilized under the specific scheme.
However, the same were reappropriated at the RE stage and utilized in some other schemes.
9.3.0    The Committee feels that the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces is taking proper care for strengthening
infrastructure and intelligence network in the States bordering Nepal. However, in light of the recent spurt in Maoist
violence in Nepal and its percolation to bordering States affected by Naxalism, the Ministry should take special
measures to strengthen Policing on the Indo-Nepal Border.
9.3.1    The Committee also recommends for empowering and strengthening of SSB, the border guarding force on the
Indo-Nepal border so as to curb not only the ISI activities through this route but also the Maoist groups in assisting the
MCC. It also feels that the Ministry should explore the possibility of amending the Indo-Nepal Treaty so as to make it
compulsory for everybody crossing the border to have his identity proof.

Modernisation of Police Forces
11.0     “Police” being a State Subject, its modernisation is the primary responsibility of the State Governments.
However, the Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for Modernization of State Police
Forces since 1969-70 to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in modernizing their police forces. The
Scheme provided assistance to the State Governments on 50% “Grants-In-Aid” and 50% loan basis. In view of the
changing situation of internal security in the country, the annual Central assistance under the scheme was pegged at
Rs.1000 crore in 2000-01 which was further enhanced to Rs. 1400 crore from 2003-04. While enhancing the annual
Central allocation during 2003-04, it was also decided to give the Central assistance only as “Grants-in-Aid”. The cost-
sharing basis was also changed by grouping the States into three categories A, B1 and B2 depending on the level of
insurgency/terrorism including cross-border terrorism being faced by the State and the funding pattern was decided as
100%, 75% and 60% respectively to these three categories of States. The Ministry is further considering the
recommendation of the Committee to group all the States in two categories (A&B) only.
11.1     On being asked about the effectiveness of the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces of the States, the
Ministry has stated that the Scheme has made perceptible impact, as proper buildings for police stations/outposts taken
up under the Scheme has provided safe and secure environment, construction of houses for police personnel and
provision of modern weaponry have boosted their morale. From the reports made available by the States and as per the
interim impact assessment report submitted by the Bureau of Police Research & Development (BPR&D), the scheme
has performed well during the last three years and it has made perceptible changes in police mobility, communication,
weapons, housing satisfaction level and Police Station buildings. Besides that, according to BPR&D, the forensic
science laboratories in the States are getting modernized also; for instance, the State Forensic Science Laboratory of
Andhra Pradesh got ISO-9002 Certificate also. Forensic Science Laboratory in Gujarat could add Brain-mapping and
Narco-analysis. State Government of Andhra Pradesh could launch an ambitious computerization project named E-cops.
Gujarat, Haryana and West Bengal have established Wide Area Networks. Training infrastructure in most States
particularly Assam and Haryana have been upgraded. State police are now being provided bullet­ proof vehicles, mine
protected vehicles, bomb detection and disposal equipment. Modern control rooms have been set at major cities. Reports
received from the States also indicate that enhanced mobility and provision of modern communication equipment have
brought down response time of the police force.

Police Grant No. 54
12.0     There has been an incremental growth since 2003 in Grant No. 54:Police. The increase is 19.78 percent in the
BE 2005-06 as compared to BE 2004-05. The Ministry has stated that it is mainly due to new raisings and
modernization of CPFs (Rs. 1000 crore) and construction of residential accommodation and official buildings for CPFs
and Delhi Police (Rs. 185 crore).      
12.1     In view of this increased allocation for police under Grant No. 54, the issue of the image of the police in public
perception was raised. It was stated that despite large allocations for modernisation of police forces in the country, the
police which has failed to project its people friendly image and the common man is deterred from going to a police
station for seeking their assistance in redressal of grievances for booking the culprits who commit crimes of various
types and for protection of lives and properties.
12.2     The Home Secretary while deposing before the Committee stated that this aspect has been considered by
different Commissions, which have made valuable recommendations. Though the process of implementation of those
recommendations is ongoing, a lot reforms need to be carried out for improving the image of the Police.
12.3     The Committee has taken note of the increasing expenditure on the head ’Police’ which constitute approximately
67 per cent of the total budget of the Ministry of Home Affairs, besides on an average Rs. 800 crore per year is being
spent for modernisation of Police Forces of States during the last three years. While endorsing the increased outlay on
the Police, the Committee feels that despite the Parliament voting such a large outlay on Police, there is no perceptible
improvement in the behavioral and attitudinal aspects of the Police personnel, which needs proper training at all levels.
12.4     The Committee, therefore strongly recommends that the Ministry should initiate sincere efforts towards
improving the police-people relationship. It also recommends that an impact analysis of the performance of the Police in
terms of crime rate, police-population ratio, satisfaction rate of people with regard to performance of police should be
undertaken and all out efforts should be made to improve and enhance the image of the Police.
Issue of Bru Refugees
13.0     There were reports of large-scale migration of Bru (Reang) families from Western Mizoram into Northern
Tripura from October 1997 onwards, allegedly due to attacks on minority Reang tribals by Mizo villagers. Since then
they have been in Tripura as refugees.
13.1     The Ministry has stated that it has been making sincere and vigorous efforts for the repatriation of those refugees
to Mizoram. On the suggestion of Ministry of Home Affairs, State Government of Mizoram has been discussing with
Bru National Liberation Front (BNLF) leaders. A scheme for laying down of arms and surrender of cadres of BNLF,
schemes for rehabilitation and resettlement of BNLF returnees and Bru refugees and a special development project for
western belt of Mizoram covering Bru settlement areas is being contemplated. So far twelve rounds of talks have been
held between representatives of Government of Mizoram and BNLF. The Government of Mizoram has since prepared a
draft agreement to be signed with BNLF leaders. It is expected that the Government of Mizoram would be signing this
agreement with BNLF leaders very soon.

grants-in-aid of Rs. 14.84 crore to Government of Mizoram includes grant-in-aid of

counter insurgency operations in Mizoram, grants-in-aid of Rs. 3.11 crore for ex-gratia payment to legal heirs of persons
killed during insurgency in Mizoram and Rs. 8 crore as first instalment of grant-in-aid to Government of Mizoram for
rehabilitation and resettlement of about 195 BNLF returnees and approximately 5000 families of Bru (Reang) refugees
The rehabilitation and resettlement of BNLF returnees/Bru refugees has not yet started, as the repatriation of BNLF

Special Assistance to States     
14.0     The Central Government is implementing a scheme for reimbursement of Security Related Expenditure (SRE) of
the States seriously affected by insurgency. This scheme covers the North Eastern States, Jammu & Kashmir and the
States affected by Naxalism. Under this scheme, the States have to first incur the expenditure and then claim
reimbursement from the Central Government. Also, only 50 per cent of the expenditure was being reimbursed. Hence,
most of the States did not make full use of this scheme.
14.1     Taking this into account, it was decided to comprehensively revise the SRE Scheme in 
2003-04.The SRE Scheme has now been revamped in February 2005 to cover more districts (76 naxal affected) and
more items.
            (i)         Insurance for State Police personnel involved in anti-naxalite operations.           
            (ii)        Lumpsum grant of up to Rs. 2 lakh to Village Defence Committees/Nagrik Surakasha Samitis for
security related expenditure.
            (iii)       Honorarium to Special Police Officers (SPOs) in naxal affected areas.
            (iv)       Rehabilitation of surrendered Naxalites.
            (v)        Community policing.
            (vi)       Need based hiring of helicopters for anti-naxalite operations.
            Extent of reimbursement has also been revised form 50 per cent to 100 per cent (except for one item viz.
provision of logistics like accommodation, communication, camp facility, transport etc. to the CPFs deployed on anti
naxalite duties, where it is 75 per cent). There is also a provision for advance release of funds under the revised SRE
guidelines for naxal affected States. The new SRE Scheme is expected to enhance the level of utilization of funds.
14.2     The Ministry informed that the items of expenditure on which reimbursement was allowed to the naxal affected
States under the Scheme were arms and ammunition, bullet proofing of vehicles, procurement of semi-automatic and
automatic weapons, purchase of new vehicles, equipping vehicles with latest communication devices, ex-gratia payment
to the families of civilians/policemen killed and logistics support for Central Police Forces deployed in naxal affected
States for anti-naxalite operations. The items of bullet proofing of vehicles, procurement of semi-automatic and
automatic weapons, purchase of new vehicles, equipping vehicles with latest communication devices were taken away
from the SRE Scheme and included under the Police Modernisation Scheme w.e.f. 1.4.2003. In view of this, the funds
allocated under the SRE Scheme for these items were also transferred to the MPF Scheme.
14.3     The Ministry has also furnished its revised guidelines for SRE expenditure to naxal affected States under the
scheme as follows:-
            A.        Criteria for inclusion of States under the SRE Scheme:
                        (i)         Existence of and activities by one or more of the organizations (which have been declared
unlawful associations/terrorist organizations either under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 or any other
Act in the State);
                        (ii)        Enactment of legislation by a State to tackle activities of naxal extremists or similar
organizations;
                        (iii)       Raising of India Reserve Battalions by the concerned States for curbing the activities of
extremists; and
                        (iv)       Inadequate development of affected areas due to hinderances created by extremist activities.
            B.         Criteria for inclusion of districts under the SRE scheme:
                        (i)         Intensity of naxal violence over a period of five years. Exceptions can be made in some cases
where it is found that a particular district which was earlier not affected or marginally affected, has, over the past
two/three years, been reporting a large number of cases of naxal violence;
                        (ii)        The organizational consolidation attained by the various naxal outfits in the affected district.
Whether the districts are having ‘Liberated area’ or ‘guerilla zones’ where the extremist outfit(s) virtually run a parallel
administration even though the overall violence profile may not be very high;    
                        (iii)       The presence of armed dalams, their free movement and their fire power which would determine
the potentiality of an extremist outfit to commit violent acts and be a serious threat to internal security. The
sophistication in arms holding has to be a determining factor,  
                        (iv)       The spread of active mass front organizations of the naxal groups that lend constant and effective
support in terms of logistics and safe regfuge to the armed cadres, needs to be taken into consideration to judge the

CHAPTER-IV
DISASTER MANAGEMENT
Introductory
17.0     Disasters are those catastrophes, mishaps, calamities, accidents which the community itself is unable to cope
with. The occurrence of a natural hazard of sufficient magnitude capable of causing substantive loss of property/life is
known as natural disaster. Floods, droughts, cyclones, earthquakes, Tsunami, landslides, avalanches and fire hazards are
mainly the cause of natural disasters. The factors leading to a natural disaster can be meteorological, geological,
ecological, environmental, technological, etc. Besides that, in the era of growing global terrorism, there are manmade
disasters which could be caused through nuclear weapons, radioactive material chemical agents or toxic industrial
chemical and biological agents. These disasters cause loss of lives, properties, damage to livelihood, economic
hardships, environmental damage, sociological & psychological after-effects, malnutrition, distress sale of people’s
assets, etc. Thus disaster can be broadly classified under two heads, viz. natural and man-made or human induced.

India's Vulnerability
17.1     India has been traditionally vulnerable to natural disasters on account of its unique geo-climatic conditions.
Floods, droughts, cyclones, earthquakes and landslides, etc. have been recurrent phenomena. About 60 per cent of the
landmass of India is prone to earthquakes of various intensities; over 40 million hectares is prone to floods; about 8 per
cent of the total area (coastal States particularly in the East coast and Gujarat) is prone to cyclones; 68 per cent of the
area is susceptible to drought; 55 per cent of total area is in seismic Zones III - IV and is vulnerable to earthquakes and
sub Himalayan/Western Ghat is vulnerable to landslides/hailstorms/cloudbursts. In the decade 1990-2000, on an average
about 4344 people lost their lives and about 30 million people were affected by disasters every year. Considering these
geo-climatic conditions disaster management occupies an important place in the country’s policy framework. The
following Ministries have been designated Nodal Ministry for various categories of disasters as shown in the table
below:—

18.0     While making a presentation on the subject, the Home Secretary informed the Committee about the major
natural disasters occurring in the country from 1990-2005, which included four major cyclones, five earthquakes of 6
plus magnitude on the Richter Scale, Tsunami on 26 December 2004, Avalanche in February 2005 and severe floods
and droughts every year or alternate years.
18.1     He further informed the Committee that even though the primary responsibility for undertaking rescue, relief and
rehabilitation measures in the event of a disaster is that of the concerned State/UT Government, the Central Government
supplements the efforts of the State Governments by providing financial and logistic support in case of major calamities.
The existing system for disaster management in some of the major countries like USA, Australia and Japan also have
the similar pattern where federal Governments are responsible for providing financial/legislative assistance to State
units.
19.0     Despite the vulnerability, till a few years back there was neither any proper policy framework nor any
institutional mechanism in the country to deal with such type of calamities. The approach to the disaster management
hitherto was primarily relief-centric. Very little attention was paid to mitigation, preparedness and measures to reduce
the impact of disasters. It was only after the major calamities such as the super cyclone in Orissa in October, 1999 and
the Bhuj earthquake in Gujarat in January, 2001 that the Government thought of a multi-dimensional, multi-disciplinary
and multi-sectoral approach involving diverse scientific, engineering, social and financial processes. With the
emergence of terrorism as a major threat to internal security during the last two decades, the need of being prepared for
dealing with manmade disasters as well in an effective and professional manner was felt imminent. Since the man-made
disaster poses threat to national security, Ministry of Home Affairs also shares responsibility for its management. The
other Ministries/ Departments/’ Organisations involved in the management of disasters are :—
            (i)         Central Water Commission (CWC)
                (ii)        Ministry of Agriculture
                (iii)       Ministry of Defence
            (iv)       Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
            (v)        Ministry of Atomic Energy
            (vi)       Indian Meteorological Department (1MD)
            (vii)      National Remote Sensing Agency
            (viii)      Indian Space Research Organization (1SRO)
19.1     Replying to a query, the Ministry has stated that there has been a shift in focus from relief centric to encompass
the entire cycle of disaster management like prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response and relief The new approach
proceeds from the conviction that development cannot be sustainable unless disaster mitigation is built into the

development process. Mitigation has to be multi-disciplinary spanning across all sectors of development.         
History of disaster management policy
19.2     The history of the Disaster Management Policy framework can be traced when a High Powered Committee was
constituted on Disaster Management under the Chairmanship of the then Secretary Agriculture, Government of India on
20 August 1999 to review existing arrangements for preparedness and mitigation of natural disasters. The Committee
recommended measures for strengthening the organizational structures and to formulate a comprehensive model plan
for Natural and Manmade Disaster Management at the National, State and District levels.
19.3     In the wake of the Bhuj Earthquake, an All Party National Committee on Disaster Management (NCDM) was
constituted under the Chairmanship of the then Prime Minister on 13 February 2001 to suggest short-term, medium-term
and long-term steps for relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction in the earthquake affected areas of Gujarat; deliberate on
the necessary institutional and legislative measures needed for an effective and long-term strategy to deal with natural
calamities in the future; and to look into the parameters that should define a natural calamity. On the recommendation of
the NCDM, in February 2002, the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 were amended to transfer
the work relating to Disaster Management, except drought, from the Ministry of Agriculture to the Ministry of Home
Affairs which actually took place in June 2002.      
19.4     The recent steps being taken by the Government in disaster management emanate from the approach as outlined
above. This approach has been translated into a National Disaster Management Framework. Keeping this objective in
view, the Government propose to enact a law on disaster management which will provide requisite institutional and
coordinated mechanism and powers for undertaking prevention and mitigation measures for ensuring preparedness and
capacity building to handle disasters. The proposed law will provide coordinated mechanism by constitution of a
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) at National level; State Disaster Management Authority at State
level; District Disaster Management Authority at district level; and the local authority at local level. The local authority
includes Corporations and Municipalities in urban areas and Zilla Parishads/Gram Panachyats in rural areas to enable
the elected representatives to discharge a key role in disaster management.
19.5     Replying to a query, the Ministry has stated that the new approach lays emphasis on (i) awareness generation,
(ii) formulation of disaster management plans, (iii) standard operating procedures (SOPs) for hazard-specific response,
(iv) strengthening of Control Rooms, (v) training of Disaster Management Teams at all levels, (vi) organizing mock
drills and (vii) establishment of search and rescue teams following a multi-pronged approach.  
19.6     Tsunami disaster, being the first of its type in India, had an element of surprise. While local administration got
into action immediately, State Governments organized rescue and relief assistance in the affected districts quickly.
Mobilization of national resources was also swift in view of the magnitude of the disaster. The flow of information,
which is extremely crucial for decision making from local level to the national level, through various Control Rooms,
was very smooth. In the post-Tsunami phase, mobilization of resources for rescue, relief and rehabilitation was
facilitated by the India Disaster Resource Network, (IDRN) an electronic web based inventory of Disaster Response
Resources.
19.7     The role of the State Government, which is primarily responsible for disaster management in the State, is to
undertake various activities in the areas of prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, relief and rehabilitation. The
Ministry has stated that it: being the nodal Ministry for Disaster Management, supplements the efforts of State/UT
Governments and coordinates Central Government’s action on all the aspects of disaster management in consultation
with the nodal Department for Disaster Management in the State Governments/UT Administrations. At the State level,
the Department of Relief and Rehabilitation, now being renamed as Department of Disaster Management is an
indication of the change in approach of being pro-active rather than reactive. The Ministry of Home Affairs is in regular
touch with the State Departments of Disaster Management and it facilitates action by various
Ministries/Departments/Agencies of the Government of India. Central Government is providing technical and financial
assistance to the State Governments for prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, relief and rehabilitation. This
well-coordinated mechanism between the States and the Central Government ensures that there are no overlaps.
National policy on disaster management
20.0     The Ministry has informed that the National Policy on Disaster Management, which is at present under
finalization, will be submitted to a Group of Experts to be constituted for this purpose. After getting the inputs from the
Group of Experts, the draft Policy on Disaster Management will be placed before the proposed National Disaster
Management Authority, which is likely to be constituted shortly, for consideration. Thereafter, approval of Cabinet will
be solicited. The policy will be finalized and submitted to the Group of Experts by 30 June 2005. The Ministry believes
that the policy is likely to be put in place by 31st December, 2005.

20.1     The Committee, while appreciating the recent efforts of the Government in putting in place a disaster

Disaster Management Authority. As mentioned by the Ministry, the National Policy on Disaster Management has to
pass through several stages before coming to the Cabinet for final approval. The Committee feels that the Ministry
should speed up the processes leading to finalisation of the National Policy. Keeping in view the geographical
vulnerability and recurrent natural disasters in India, the Committee urges the Ministry to lay the Policy in Parliament at
the earliest so that the Disaster Management Authority could immediately implement the same.
Three tier policy-Mapping, Coordination, Implementation system
21.0     The Committee was informed that at the apex level, there are two Cabinet Committees, one on Natural
Calamities and the other on Security. Major issues relating to natural disasters are placed before the Cabinet Committee
on Natural Calamities for decisions. In case of calamities which impinge on internal security or which may be caused
due to use of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons/materials, the matters are placed before the Cabinet Committee
on Security.
21.1     The Cabinet Committee on Disaster Management (CCDM) is headed by the Prime Minister. The National Crisis
Management Committee (NCMC) is headed by the Cabinet Secretary. While the Crisis Management Group (CMG) is in
the Ministry of Home Affairs, which is the nodal Ministry for response and relief in the event of natural and manmade
disasters, the Central Relief Commissioner in the Ministry of Home Affairs is the Chairperson of CMG. All the three
levels are part of the disaster management mechanism and are activated depending upon the severity of the disaster and
the national efforts required for providing necessary support to the States. There is a regular and coordinated interaction,
in this institutional mechanism, during a period of crisis.

through Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) which is based on the recommendation of Eleventh Finance Commission for 2000-
2005 and Twelfth Finance Commission for 2005-2010 which is available to States for immediate relief and
rehabilitation. But if the disaster is of a very high magnitude then relief is provided from National Calamity
Contingency Fund (NCCF) on the recommendation of the Inter Ministerial Group headed by Agriculture Minister.
Money from NCCF can be granted by the Union Government to the States once the States exhaust the money from their
share in the CRF.

training of Special Response Team (SRTs) and other commitments in a short span of time.
24.10   It was suggested that while the Government was spending so much on disaster management, it should provide
some mechanism to spend the fund efficiently, to have a long term planning to equip the people, communities to deal
with recurrent disasters rather than being reactive to the disaster in fire fighting manner. It was also suggested that
buildings especially in metros should compulsorily have bomb shelters.
24.11   The Committee raised the point regarding legislative sanction by modifying building bye-laws to construct
earthquake resistant buildings so as to restrict the damage to which the expert on Risk Reduction from Natural
Calamities agreed and stated that steps were being taken in this regard.
24.12   The Committee appreciates the efforts being made to give legislative sanction to building bye-laws. The
Committee is of the view that guidelines should be issued to the State and Local authorities indicating the parameters for
construction of earthquake resistant buildings/structures.
25.0     The Committee while taking note of the savings of Rs. 10.57 crore allocated for disaster management during
2004-05 observes that it belies sincerity on the part of the Ministry and recommends that funds allocated for this
important purpose should be utilised properly in the future.
25.1     It appeared quite unusual to the Committee that the work relating to Disaster Management has been transferred
to the Ministry of Home Affairs but the Group of Ministers for deciding grants to States from NCCF is headed by
Minister of Agriculture. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the Government may like to review this
arrangement for better co-ordination.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
 
REHABILITATION OF J&K MIGRANTS AND SECURITY RELATED EXPENDITURE (SRE)
            The Committee expresses its deep concern over the living conditions in rehabilitation camps of Kashmiri
migrants in Jammu and Delhi and Government’s dilemma and lack of clear vision on the future of these migrants. The
Committee is of the considered view that the migrants should be sent back to the Valley only when adequate security of
their lives and properties is ensured. Keeping in view the living conditions in the camps, the Committee feels that
Government instead of projecting a saving Rs. 174 crore under Relief and Rehabilitation, should have utilised the full
amount allocated under the said head for improving the living condition in these camps. The Committee is also of the
view that instead of conducting studies on migrants some concrete steps to improve their living conditions should be
taken urgently.(Para 8.4)
POLICE STRENGTHENING ON INDO-NEPAL BORDER
            The Committee feels that the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces is taking proper care for strengthening
infrastructure and intelligence network in the States bordering Nepal. However, in light of the recent spurt in Maoist
violence in Nepal and its percolation to bordering States affected by Naxalism, the Ministry should take special
measures to strengthen Policing on the Indo-Nepal Border.
                        (Para 9.3.0)
            The Committee also recommends for empowering and strengthening of SSB, the border guarding force on the
Indo-Nepal border so as to curb not only the ISI activities through this route but also the Maoist groups in assisting the
MCC. It also feels that the Ministry should explore the possibility of amending the Indo-Nepal Treaty so as to make it
compulsory for everybody crossing the border to have his identity proof.           (Para 9.3.1)
MULTI-PURPOSE NATIONAL IDENTITY CARD SCHEME
            The Committee is of the view that the shortfall of expenditure on such an important project having far-reaching
ramifications for the maintenance of internal security of the country and useful in many other areas is unacceptable and
that the Ministry should take appropriate action to complete the pilot project at the earliest so that the same may be
implemented at the national level.    (Para 10.3)

MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCES
            In the light of the fact that the scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces has a significant effect on the morale
and strength of the Police Forces of the States, the Committee endorses the proposal of the Ministry for grant of Rs.
1400 crore for the scheme for the financial year  2005-06 and therefore recommends that an additional allocation of Rs.
500 crore be made during the RE stage. It also directs the Ministry to step up its efforts towards better utilisation of the
funds under the scheme by the State Governments and that too with an emphasis on equipping of all the State Police
Forces on a balanced scale. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation as contained in its One Hundred
and Ninth Report that the States be grouped into two categories only viz. A and B for the purpose of allocation of funds
under the scheme.(Para 11.4)
POLICE GRANT NO. 54
            The Committee has taken note of the increasing expenditure on the head 'Police' which constitute approximately
67 per cent of the total budget of the Ministry of Home Affairs, besides on an average Rs. 800 crore per year is being
spent for modernisation of Police Forces of States during the last three years. While endorsing the increased outlay on
the Police, the Committee feels that despite the Parliament voting such a large outlay on Police, there is no perceptible
improvement in the behavioral and attitudinal aspects of the Police personnel, which needs proper training at all
levels.          (Para 12.3)
            The Committee, therefore strongly recommends that the Ministry should initiate sincere efforts towards
improving the police-people relationship. It also recommends that an impact analysis of the performance of the Police in
terms of crime rate, police-population ratio, satisfaction rate of people with regard to performance of police should be
undertaken and allout efforts should be made to improve and enhance the image of the Police.           (Para 12.4)
ISSUE OF BRU REFUGEES
            The Committee noted the reply of the Ministry and recommends that it should step up its efforts to repatriate and
rehabilitate Bru refugees on priority basis.          (Para 13.3)
SPECIAL ASSISTANCE TO STATES
            Considering the unsound financial position of States, the Committee appreciates the decision of the Government
to revise the scheme for reimbursing SRE from 50 per cent to 100 per cent and also the provision for advance release of
funds with respect to naxal affected States. However, it also recommends that the Government should enhance the level
of reimbursement from 
75 per cent to 100 per cent on the item relating to provision of logistics to the CPFs deployed in naxal affected States as
well as to extend the provision for advance release of funds to SRE for North East and J & K.          (Para 14.4)
            The Committee feels that considering the financial position of States affected by insurgency, terrorism and
naxalism, the Ministry should fully utilise the budgetary allocation for Special Assistance to States.       (Para 14.7)
STATUS OF IMPLEMENTATION OF ACCORDS IN THE NE REGION
            The Committee has taken note of the information furnished by the Ministry with regard to the implementation of
various accords in North-East Region. The Committee urges the Ministry to implement the various provisions of these
accords which have not yet been implemented as delay in implementation of the same adversely effect the psyche of the
people of North East and serves as a viable tool in the hands of undesirable elements to carry on a negative campaign
against the Government.            (Para 15.4)
BUDGETARY PROVISION FOR UTs WITH LEGISLATURE
            The Committee expresses its serious concern that under the present set up it may not be feasible for the Union
Territory Administrations to raise money from open market as recommended by the Twelfth Finance Commission. In
such circumstances insufficient budgetary provision may create serious financial crunch for the UTs. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that keeping in view the financial constraints of the Union Territories, the Ministry should
urgently set up enabling institutional mechanism in the Union Territories for facilitating borrowing from open
market.        (Para 16.2)
NATIONAL POLICY ON DISASTER MANAGEMENT
            The Committee, while appreciating the recent efforts of the Government in putting in place a disaster
management mechanism at the national level, notes that a lot of exercise has already been done at the governmental
level during the last three years starting from the constitution of the High Powered Committee to the setting up of a
Disaster Management Authority. As mentioned by the Ministry, the National Policy on Disaster Management has to
pass through several stages before coming to the Cabinet for final approval. The Committee feels that the Ministry
should speed up the processes leading to finalisation of the National Policy. Keeping in view the geographical
vulnerability and recurrent natural disasters in India, the Committee urges the Ministry to lay the Policy in Parliament at
the earliest so that the Disaster Management Authority could immediately implement the same.           (Para 20.1)

DISASTER RESPONSE FORCE
            The Committee observes that the pace of preparation for management of man-made disaster is also very slow
and that no concrete action plan has so far been prepared and that the same should be expedited.           (Para 22.3.1)
            The Committee, while noting the responsibility of different Ministries for handling different disasters under the
Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 observes that the allocation of subjects to various Ministries were formulated when
there was no such holistic concept of disaster management. Hence, in the light of new developments, the Committee
feels that there should be mention in the Allocation of Business Rules of emergency support function of Ministry of
Home Affairs to provide necessary logistic and other supports to the different nodal Ministries associated with
management of different types of disasters so as to take care of any ambiguity in this important matter.      (Para 24.2)

CHAPTER-1
Overview
         The North-Eastern Region comprising the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram,
Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim has lagged behind the rest of the country as far as development is concerned. As a result,
it has been the focal point of Special Assistance of the Central Government, particularly during the last few years. In
that genre, a separate Department of Development of North-East Region was created in September, 2001. Later on, a
full-fledged dedicated Ministry designated as Ministry of Development of North-East Region (DoNER) was created
w.e.f. 27th May, 2004.
2.      In the National Common Minimum Programme (CMP) all North-Eastern States are to be given Special Assistance
to upgrade and expand infrastructure. The North­-Eastern Council is to be strengthened and given adequate
professional support. It also talks of a Special Economic Package announced for the North East to be implemented
expeditiously. It accords priority to the development and expansion of physical infrastructure like roads, highways,
power, water supply etc.
3.      To fulfil the above objectives, the Ministry of DoNER has following subjects under its remit:­
(i)     Matters of planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes and projects of North Eastern
Region including those in the sectors of Power, Irrigation, Roads and Communications;
(ii)     Hill Area Development Programme and Border Area Development Programme in North Eastern Region;
(iii)    Non-lapsable Fund for the North Eastern Region;
(iv)    North Eastern Council;
(v)    North Eastern Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi)
(vi)    North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited (NERAMAC);
(vii)   The Sikkim Mining Corporation Limited (SMC);
(viii) North Eastern Handlooms and Handicrafts Development Corporation (NEHHDC), Shillong;
(ix)    Road works financed in whole or in part by the Central Government in the North Eastern Region; and
(x)    Planning of Road and Inland Waterways Transport in the North Eastern Region.
4.      The Ministry is headed by a Cabinet Minister and supported by one Secretary and three Joint Secretaries among
other officers. The Ministry has the following three broad divisions:-
(i)     Policy and Programme Division: It looks after Policy formulation, Cabinet and PMO matters, Coordination
with Central Ministries/Departments and State Governments, International Corporation, North Eastern
Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi), North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation
Limited (NERAMAC), North Eastern Handicrafts and Handloom Development Corporation Limited
(NEHHDC), Inland Waterways, Business Summit, Private Sector Investment and Parliamentary Work. This
Division also looks after Plans and Budget and Administration of the Ministry.
(ii)     NLP Division : It looks after the work of administration of the Non Lapsable Central Pool of Resources
(NLCPR).
(iii)    NEC Division : It looks after North Eastern Council, Schemes of Technical Assistance, Advocacy and
Publicity, Hill Area Development Programme, Border Area Development Programme and Information
Technology. This Division also looks after the work of Sikkim Mining Corporation.
5.      The Ministry has formulated four Central Plan Schemes. They are Advocacy and Publicity, Capacity Building,
Assistance to Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) and North Eastern Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi). In the
plans of the North -Eastern States, grants from Non Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) and scheme for North
Eastern Council (NEC) are included. The Projects for Infrastructure Development under NLCPR are
identified/prioritized by the State Governments and submitted to the Ministry of DoNER. The NEC provides financial
assistance for regional infrastructure projects like construction of roads, improving air connectivity, assistance to
regional medical colleges etc.

6.0    Prime Ministers' Package - Prime Ministers during their visit to the North Eastern Region from time to time have
announced socio-economic packages for the development of the Region. These packages are implemented by the
concerned Ministries/Departments/Organizations of the Central Government. The Ministry of DoNER implemented
certain schemes/programmes under the following packages:­
(i)     Socio-Economic Package for the North Eastern Region as announced by the then Prime Minister Shri A.B.
Vajpayee in January, 2000 at Shillong.
(ii)     Socio-Economic Package for Sikkim announced by the then Prime Minister Shri A.B. Vajpayee at Gangtok
on 13.4.2003
(iii)    Socio-Economic Package for Nagaland announced by the then Prime Minister Shri A.B. Vajpayee at
Kohima in October, 2003
6.1    The implementation of the Schemes and Programmes in the Agenda for Socio­-Economic Development of the
North Eastern States and Sikkim are being monitored and reviewed by the Prime Minister’s Office and also by the
Ministry for Development of NE Region with the concerned implementing Ministries/Departments/Agencies.
7.0    PROGRAMMES OF THE MINISTRY
7.1    Hill Area Development Programme (HADP)- The main objective of the programme is sustainable development
in the hilly areas by eco-preservation and eco­ restoration with emphasis on preservation of bio-diversity and
rejuvenation of the hill ecology. At present, HADP is being implemented in two Hill Districts of Assam.
7.2    Border Areas Development Programme (BADP)- It is 100 per cent Centrally funded special area programme,
which covers border blocks of the North Eastern States having international borders. This programme is carried out in
the seventeen States of the country including States of the NER. The broad objective of the programme is to meet
special needs of the people living in the remote and inaccessible areas situated near international border.
8.0    SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
8.1    Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) - The Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR)
became operational in April, 1998 due to the fact that there were short falls in the stipulated expenditure norm of 10 per
cent of the Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) by some Union Ministries/Departments for supporting infrastructure
development projects of the North East. Enhancement of the budgetary provision for new infrastructural
projects/schemes and its speedy implementation are the broad objectives of the NLCPR schemes. Both economic and
social sectors projects like Power, Roads and Bridges, Education, Health, Water Supply are considered for funding
under the Central Pool.
8.2    Advocacy and Publicity ----- The Plan Scheme of Advocacy and Publicity has been formulated to highlight the
inherent potentials and achievements, in social, economic and cultural sectors, of the people of the North Eastern
Region and to expose their best practices to the rest of the country. It also seeks to highlight the role of Government in
catalyzing the development process.
8.3    Capacity Building ----- Capacity Building and Technical Assistance to the North Eastern States is a key mandate
of the Ministry. Under this scheme, the Ministry has formulated a plan focusing on development, in consonance with the
people’s wishes and aspirations. The Capacity Building plan scheme was formulated with a view to filling the gap in the
Technical and Management skills required for the development of the Region. The emphasis is on the participation of
people in the developmental process.
9.0.   ATTACHED BODIES AND PUBLIC SECTOR UNITS OF THE MINISTRY
9.l .0 North Eastern Council (NEC) - The North Eastern Council (NEC) is a statutory body, created under an Act of
Parliament. The Council functions as a Regional Planning Body for securing the balanced development of the North
Eastern Region and for Inter­ State coordination. NEC is mandated to plan, implement and manage regional projects. It
is also entrusted with the task of reviewing the measures taken by the North Eastern States for the maintenance of
security and public order in the region. Under NEC, special emphasis is on the projects/schemes, which will benefit two
or more States. In addition, the NEC will also review the implementation of projects/schemes and recommend measures
for effective coordination in the matter of implementation.
9.1.1 On the Revitalization of NEC, the Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri P.P Srivastava had submitted its
report on 30th July 2004, which inter alia recommended a series of measures for operationalising the new mandate of
the North Eastern Council. These include composition of Council, organizational set up, regional planning for

Trade and review of measures taken by the States for maintenance of security and public order in the Region. The
Government of India has, by and large, accepted the recommendations of the Committee. It has also accepted the

9.2    North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Ltd. (NEDFi) ----- North Eastern Development Finance
Corporation is a financial institution supporting entrepreneurs in the region by sanctioning projects and disbursement of
loans. During the Tenth Plan Rs. 100 crore is being given to NEDFi in the form of a soft loan to increase its liquidity,
which is repayable as bullet repayment at the end of the Tenth Plan.
9.3    North Eastern Handicrafts and Handloom Development Corporation Ltd. (NEHHDC) ----- The main
objective of the NEHHDC is to develop and promote handicrafts, handlooms and allied projects of the North Eastern
Region and the welfare of the indigenous artisans and weavers. NEHHDC was incorporated on 31 March 1977 as a
Central Public Sector Undertaking and is owned by the Government of India. Currently, the corporation is running in
losses and the net loss is 1.90 crore in the current financial year, whereas the turnover the Corporation during April
2004- January 2005 was Rs 6.50 crore.
9.4    North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. (NERAMAC)  ----- NERAMAC is
expected to build up marketing infrastructure, processing facilities and providing assistance in marketing arrangement
for agro/horticulture products of the region. The corporation has also been associated in programmes of helping the
farmers of the region in making them aware about the competitive prices for their produce and organizing training for
technical know-how on commercial aspects.
9.5    Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) ----- Sikkim Mining Corporation (SMC) was constituted for the purpose of
developing the deposits of copper, lead, zinc and other minerals in Bhotang and other places in Sikkim. This joint
venture between the Government of Sikkim (51%) and Government of India (49%) has been operating at a loss.

CHAPTER - III
Policies, Programmes and Schemes of the Ministry
Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR)
13.0  The Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) came into existence in      April, 1998 for supporting
infrastructure development projects in the North East. The NLCPR are accrued from the unspent balance of the
mandatory provision of 10 per cent            of Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) made for the North Eastern Region in the
Budget of Central Ministries/Departments.
13.1  The main objective of the NLCPR is to ensure speedy development of infrastructure in NER by increasing the
How of budgetary provision for new infrastructure projects/schemes, both in economic and social sectors such as
Power, Roads and Bridges, Education, Health, Water Supply and Sanitation. Funds from Central Pool are available for
State sector as well as Central sector projects/schemes.
13.2  The Planning and Development Department of the North Eastern States is the nodal Department for NLCPR and is
DoNER’s interface with all other Departments of these States. The NE States through these Departments submit
prioritized list of projects to the interdepartmental NLCPR committee headed by Secretary, Ministry of DoNER. That
Committee selects projects out of the prioritized list for retention. After the approval of the Ministry of DoNER,
Detailed Project Reports are obtained from the respective State Governments for getting examined by Ministry for

budgetary support to 10 per cent loan component to States. The Committee has doubt about the capacity of these special

13.6  The Committee expressed its concern with regard to the decision of the Government for not providing ten per cent

from the market.
13.7  The Committee notes the trend of constant increase in the utilization of 10 per cent of the Gross Budgetary
Support of various Ministries/Departments for the development of the NER as is demonstrated by increase in
expenditure from 6.71 per cent in 1998-99 to 8.34 per cent in 2003-04. So far fifteen Ministries/Department are able to
spend the total ten per cent of their plan budget for the NER. lf that trend continues, the corpus fund, which now stands
at Rs. 3643 crore, would be exhausted within a period of next four to five years. The Committee visualises a situation
when 
10 per cent earmarked funds are fully utilized by the concerned Central Ministries and there will be no funds in NLCPR.
The Committee is of the view that the Planning Commission should take note of such a situation and should make some
budgetary allocation for smooth implementation of NLCPR projects at that time.

committed to provide all NE States, special assistance to upgrade and expand infrastructure. The Committee was also
informed that a number of economically viable projects, which were also socially important, could not be implemented
due to inadequate allocation of funds by Ministry of Finance in the Annual Plan Outlay.

apprehension of the fact that how the Government would be able to meet the basic, immediate and foremost need of the
region as committed in CMP, with lower allocations from the NLCPR. The Committee strongly recommends that

14.0  The Committee was informed that the North Eastern Council reorganized in June 2003 by which the NEC was
made Regional Planning Body. The organisation has been further revitalized recently in 2005. The CMP of the
Government also intends to strengthen and give adequate professional support to the NEC.
14.1  As part of the programme to revitalise NEC, the Minister of DoNER has been made the Chairman of the NEC and
a Member of the Planning Commission has been made an ex-officio member of the NEC to give better input to the body.
Besides him, two other members having good experience and expertise about the NER have been made the members of
the NEC.
14.2  The Committee pointed out that the support to the NEC should not be individualized rather professional support in
the form of institution should come to the NEC for its better functioning as Regional Planning Body, which would
enable the Council to utilise limited resources with most profitable manner.
14.3  It was pointed out during the course of meetings that no Road Map/Masterplan has been prepared for overall
socio-economic development of the North Eastern Region during the last three decades.
14.4  The Secretary, North Eastern Council, in response thereto, stated that the reorganised North Eastern Council is
contemplating to draw a Blue Print for formulation of a comprehensive Road Map for speedy socio-economic
upliftment of the North Eastern Region. A “North East Vision-2020” - Document is also under the preparation of the
North Eastern Council. As the regional planner, reorientation of the NEC has been undertaken in its approach to speed
up socio-economic development by following ways:
(i)     Private/public sector participation in socio-economically beneficial and commercially viable projects;
(ii)     Increase credibility among the public, government agencies, financial institutions and opinion builders;
(iii)    Mobilise resources through joint-ventures;
(iv)    Promote NER as united entity;
(v)    Mission mode approach for:
a.      ICT
b.      Non-conventional energy
c.      Cluster approach
d.      Small and rural business,
e.      Tourism
f.       Bamboo
g.      Village & small enterprises
h.      Voluntary action cell
i.       Rural Technologies
j.       Marketing
k.      Herbs and aromatics
l.       Handloom and Handicraft
m.     Food processing
n.      KVI sector,
o.      Infrastructure leasing and investment
         (vi)    Use professional agencies like ILFS etc.
14.5  The Committee has noted the change in approach with respect to the functioning of the North Eastern Council and
urges the Ministry to give due consideration to those factors which enable the North Eastern Council to play an effective

113th Report of Committee on Home Affairs

role in the development of the North Eastern Region.
14.6  Some Members felt the need of watchdog to oversee the progress of projects sanctioned by the NEC. They desire
that there should be a think tank in the NEC to properly monitor and evaluate the projects
14.7  The Secretary, NEC appraised the Committee about strengthening of the monitoring and evaluation unit of the
NEC, restructuring of its Secretariat to make it think tank of regional planning and for that purpose 50 per cent of the
officers would be outsourced. Further, link Officers for each Member States would be appointed to act for better
coordination and effective monitoring.
14.8  The Committee while noting the reply of the Secretary, NEC desires that the proposal enumerated above should be
implemented at the earliest to pave the way for the speedy development for the NER
Border Area Development Programme (BADP)
15.0  The Border Area Development Programme (BADP) for the NER, is a hundred per cent centrally funded
programme, which has been transferred to the Ministry of DoNER from the Ministry of Home Affairs. It covers Border
Blocks of the NE States having international Borders with Bangladesh, Myanmar, China and Bhutan. Funds are
provided on hundred per cent grants basis. The main objective of the programme is to provide special attention to the
needs of the people living in the inaccessible areas situated near the international border.
15.1  It was pointed out by the Committee that many a time the development under the BADP takes place in the areas,
which are very far away from the border points.
15.2  The Committee is happy to note that the BADP has been placed under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of DoNER
and observes that the development projects were confined to nodal points of the border Blocks, and areas which are
situated very near to the international border have not been included in this programme.
15.3  The Committee further opines that for better development in the border areas, which lie along the international
border of the NE States, programmes related to roads, water, medical facility etc., should be given top priority. The
Committee also feels that the budgetary allocation of Rs. 325 crore for the programme in the NE States should be
increased to atleast Rs. 500 crores.
Promotion of Tourism
16.0  The NE region is one of the most beautiful part of the country blessed with natural beauty and diverse culture but
its tourism potential has not been adequately explored neither for the domestic nor for the foreign circuit.
16.1  The Committee, in its One hundred and Tenth Report has recommended that the Ministry should tie-up with the
Ministry of Tourism to formulate perspective plan for development of tourism infrastructure.
16.2  The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Tourism has chalked out a plan for the NER by allocating Rs
52.05 crore for the year 2005-06 which is ten per cent of their GBS. The programme mainly includes publicity and
publication relating to the tremendous potential of the region, focussed marketing, generating more avenues for tourist
besides a special emphasis on Eco-tourism and Ethnic tourism.
16.3  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER in coordination with the Ministry of Tourism should
make constant efforts to explore various avenues for development of better tourism related infrastructure to attract
tourists, which would provide boost to the sagging economic condition of this region.
16.4  The Committee made a special mention of the Manas Wildlife Sanctuary and feels that this sanctuary alongwith
other numerous places of attraction in the region should be developed and the concepts such as Eco Tourism, Ethnic
Tourism and Buddhist Monasteries have the potentials to bring this region on the tourist map of the world.
Upliftment of Civil Aviation infrastructure in NER
17.0  The Committee is of the view that the infrastructure development programmes relating to Tourism would be futile
in absence of providing better connectivity to the region, whether it is within the NE States or with the rest of the
country. Lack of proper road and rail transportation system coupled with its uneven terrain makes air travel as the best
option for communication. Well-equipped airports will provide further encouragement for the transportation in this
region.
17.1. The Committee takes note of the fact that out of the 26 airports of the NER, only 11 are in the working condition.
The Committee has been apprised that a business like approach has been initiated to improve the airports in NER.
Several private investors have been consulted in this regard. The Committee was also informed that NEC, the regional

113th Report of Committee on Home Affairs

planning body for NE States in its ‘Mission Mode’ programme has given priority to the upliftment of the airports of the
region.
17.2  The Committee while taking note of the efforts of the Ministry regarding the development of Civil Aviation
infrastructure including Airports, opined that still a lot more needs to be done to improve the quality of airports for
developing better air connectivity. The Committee also suggested that better connectivity of each State of NE would
also provide an opportunity for the marketing of cash crops, which are perishable in nature, not only within the NE
States but also in the other parts of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the projects concerning
development of civil aviation in this region should be taken up on priority basis and more funds should be allocated for
early completion of those projects.
Modernization of Road Network
18.0  One of the Members of the Committee pointed out that the Road network especially the North East Express
Highway is in deplorable condition and needs immediate and utmost repair works. A Member of the Committee pointed
out that inter state roads between Meghalaya and Assam is in worst condition and no maintenance is being done either
by the NEC or by the State PWD.
l8.1   In this regard the Committee was informed that the responsibility of maintenance of roads lay with the NEC
alongwith respective State Governments. Rs. l4 crore had been sanctioned for maintenance of 6000 km. stretch of road,
which had been constructed during last two years by NEC. The Committee was further apprised that for the inter-state
road between Meghalaya and Assam, Rs. 40 lakh had been sanctioned for maintenance.
18.2  The Committee notes that upon an analysis of the allocation of money made for maintenance of roads constructed
during last two years by NEC i.e, Rs. 14 crore for 6000 km., it works out to 
Rs. 24 per metre which appears to be meagre as it makes the maintenance of road non-feasible. The Committee is,
therefore, of the view that keeping in mind the uneven terrain and seasonal variations of the NER, a large sum of money
is needed for proper maintenance and further construction of the road network. The Committee has also been apprised
of the North East Road Development Project, an externally aided project sanctioned by Asian Development Bank
(ADB) and the progress made in this regard. The Committee opines that more such progremmes are needed in NER and
also recommends that the issue of maintenance and construction of new roads should be taken up with the State PWD
for better implementation of the projects specially the North East Express Highway. It also feels that this project should
be taken up on priority basis and more funds should be allocated for early completion of the entire road network of the
NER.
Development of Autonomous District Council
19.0  The Sixth Schedule of the constitution provides for provision to the administration of tribal Areas in the NE States.
These provisions shall apply to the administration regarding the Scheduled Area and Scheduled Tribes of NE States.
They are identified as Autonomous District Council Area and are entrusted to advise on         matters pertaining to the
welfare and advancement of the Schedule Tribes in the State.
19.1  The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee stated that the Ministry of DoNER had sanctioned 72
projects for Autonomous District Council area in the NE States. He further submitted that most of these projects are
sanctioned for Bodoland Autonomous Council Area whereas 10 projects are sanctioned for Karbi Anglong Autonomous
District Council and 9 projects for North Cachar Hills Autonomous District Council.
19.2  The Committee understands that development of the Autonomous District Council areas is long overdue. These
areas are identified & included in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution so as to devote special attention to them as they
are lagging behind the rest of the NER both in social & economic development.
19.3  Members of the Committee belonging to the NE States have very strongly raised the issue that the Autonomous
District Council areas are not getting any kind of benefits out of the Ministry of DoNER as well as North Eastern
Council. The Council hardly sanctions any developmental projects for autonomous District Council. Even in NLCPR
projects only Bodo-land Territorial Council Area (BTC) caught the attention of the Ministry and get the budgetary
provision of Rs. 100 crore, which is quite insufficient as the BTC comprises of four districts. And the amount allocated
for each district comes to Rs. 25 crore only, which is too meagre for the developmental work required in these most
backward regions of the NER.
19.4  The Committee recommends that special allocation needs to be made for the overall development of this region.
Planning for these areas should be done keeping in mind the classification of the areas as the Most Backward, Backward
and Developing areas. The geographical factors and the seasonal variation should also be taken into account while

implementing the projects. Identification of core sectors is also essential, for overall development of infrastructure of the
area.
Implementation Mechanism
20.0  During the discussion on Demands for Grants, the issue of insurgency was highlighted by one of the Members of
the Committee. The Secretary, Ministry of DoNER             stated that no project has been reportedly hampered till now
due to the insurgency factor. The Committee was informed that the Ministry is further strengthening the monitoring and
evaluation mechanism. The Ministry has further stated that NEC is facilitating consultation on an ongoing basis on
security related aspect in the implementation of the project. The NEC is planning to develop Link Office System, which
would work as a linkage between security concern and development.
20.1  The Committee is of the view that the implementation of projects is tardy inspite of best efforts made by the
Ministry. The Committee in this regard recommends that the Ministry should constantly endeavour to improve upon the
monitoring and evaluation mechanism. The Committee even suggests that a nodal office of the Ministry of DoNER
might be established in the NER for better monitoring of projects: A strict and regular on-the-spot assessment of the
actual implementation should be done by the concerned agencies in the State to ensure proper execution of all the
projects.
Miscellanous
21.0  The Committee takes serious view on the lowest per capita income of the people of NE States and skeptical about
the benefits for the various developmental programmes reaching to general public. The Committee thinks that the
progress made in NE States should reflect in the increase of income of the people of North Eastern Region.
21.1  In this regard, the Committee was informed that the special category States of North East should not be equated
with the other States of the country. Special concession have to be given in regard to the North East States due to the
fact that this region has very tardy growth in its industrial and service sectors. Lack of infrastructure, peculiar
socio-­political situation prevailing there besides the ability and capacity of the States in implementing the projects is
the main reasons behind this situation.
21.2  The Committee after taking note of the special circumstances prevalent in the NER, recommends that the Ministry
should ensure equitable distribution of funds amongst NE States keeping in mind the existing inter-State and intra-State
regional disparities, Human Development Indices (HDI) including per capita income, poverty level etc. The Committee
further recommends that the entrepreneurs from within the country and outside should be encouraged to invest in the
North Eastern Region to speed up the process of its economic development.
21.3  The Committee further takes note of the ongoing border trade programme in the States, which is presently taking
place from Mureh in Manipur. The Committee suggests that more such centres could be identified so that Border-trade
between NE States and neighbouring countries could be strengthened further. The Committee feels that this exercise
will not only provide much needed boost to the marketing of agricultural products, which are perishable in nature, but
also to the agricultural/horticultural produces, which are in abundance and it will go a long way in providing an
opportunity to the related industries to expand their horizons.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS – AT A GLANCE
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS
         The Committee observes that the policy decision of the Government to stop budgeting of loan component of
Central assistance to States by encouraging them to arrange loan from market is a retrograde step for the special
category States of the NER. The Committee feels that these States may not be able to raise loans from market, which
would resultantly affect their socio-economic development. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the said policy
decision of the Government may be reviewed for the special category States of the NER and recommends that
budgetary provisions may be kept at least at the level of BE 2004-
05.                                                                                            (Para 12.0)
         The Committee notes that the pattern of release of funds from Tenth Plan to the Annual Plan of the Ministry of
DoNER is uneven. The Committee feels that it should be spread over the years evenly.                 (Para 12.1)
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
         The Committee expressed its concern with regard to the decision of the Government for not providing ten percent
budgetary support of loan component and recommends that the Ministry should pursue with the Ministry of Finance for
enhancement of the budgetary allocation by stating the difficulties that might be faced by the NE States in raising loan

2.      The Chairperson welcomed the Secretary, Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) to the
meeting of the Committee and mentioned that besides Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of DoNER an equally
important Ministry is. under the jurisdiction of the Committee and it is deeply concerned about the state of development
of North Eastern Region. The Chairperson then invited the Secretary, Ministry of DoNER to make a presentation on the
budgetary provisions of the Ministry, expenditure and shortfalls etc.
3.      The Secretary made a powerpoint presentation on Demands for Grants (2005-06) of Ministry of DoNER which
inter alia included a comparison of the BEs for 2002-03 to 2005-06; details of expenditure of various Central
Ministries/Departments under mandatory ten percent allocation from 1999-2000 to 2003-04 in NE States; percentage
         utilization of funds in the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) and NEC for the last three years. He
then elucidated upon the NLCPR projects and presented the sector-wise sanction of NLCPR projects, and utilization of
NLCPR funds by NE States. He also presented the sector- wise outlay and performance of NEC. The need for
enhancement of allocation under NLCPR and NEC budget was also shown in the presentation. The Secretary then made
a brief introduction regarding the programmes going on under two plan schemes viz Advocacy Publicity Scheme and
Capacity Building & Technical Assistant Scheme. He then apprised the Committee about the initiatives taken by the
Ministry of DoNER and progress made in respect of Externally Aided Projects in the NER. Lastly, he drew the attention

113th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/113threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:32:09]
of the Committee to the fact that significant forward movement has taken place in the developmental activities in the
NER owing to fund flow from the Ministry of DoNER and stated that developmental progress could be further
accelerated if budgetary allocation is increased.
4.      The Chairperson while thanking the Secretary for the presentation raised a query regarding the policy decision of
the Government not to provide budgetary support of ten percent as loan component of assistance to the States and
apprehends that these special category States of NER would not be able to raise funds from the market. The Chairperson
also advocated the need for additional resources of funds for the NLCPR at the time when the entire corpus were
exhausted.
4.1    Responding. to the query, the Secretary of the Ministry also expressed its concern over these issues and requested
the Committee to consider recommendation for allocation of ten per cent of budgetary support as loan component to the
special category NE States.
4.2    Members made a number of suggestions for various developmental projects going on in NER. Some Members
also raised queries regarding reasons for continuous failure implementing the projects in NER particularly in militancy
affected areas; status of the blueprint for the North East Express Highway Project; lack of maintenance or the entire road
stretch in the NER; basis on which funds were allocated to each State of NE; re-­identification of Border Areas so that
the benefits could reach to the affected people; status of Border Trade in NER; non-existence of Agricultural Promotion
