MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
         Clause 74 of the Bill provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for carrying
out the purposes of this Act.
         The rules to be made under this Bill may include the composition and number of the members of the National Authority under
sub-clause (2) of clause 3, the allowances to be paid to the members of the advisory committee under sub-clause (2) of clause 7, the
powers and functions of the Chairperson of the National Executive Committee  under sub-clause (3) of clause 8 and the procedure to
be followed by the National Executive Committee in exercise of its powers and discharge of its functions under sub-clause (4) of
clause 8, the allowances to be paid to the persons associated with the sub-committee under sub-clause (3) of clause 9, the manner of
constitution of the Force, the conditions of service of the members of the Force, including disciplinary provisions under sub-clause
(2) of clause 44, the form in which and the time within which annual report is to be prepared under clause 69, and any other matter
which is to be, or may be, prescribed, or in respect of which provision is to be made by rules under sub-clause (2) of clause 74.
2.      Clause 75 of the Bill provides that the State Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules to carry out
the provisions of this Act. The rules to be made under this Bill may include the composition and number of the members of the State
Authority under sub-clause (2) of clause 14, the allowances to be paid to the members of the advisory committee under sub-clause
(2) of clause 17 , the powers and functions of the Chairperson of the State Executive Committee under sub-clause (3) of clause 20,
and the procedure to be followed by the State Executive Committee in exercise of its powers and discharge of its functions under
sub-clause (4) of clause 20, allowances to be paid to the persons associated with the sub-committee under sub-clause (3) of clause
21, the composition and the number of members of the District Authority under sub-clause (2) of clause 25, and the powers and
functions to be exercised and discharged by the Chief Executive Officer of the District Authority under sub-clause (3) of clause 25,
any other matter which is to be, or may be, prescribed, or in respect of which provision is to be made by rules under sub-clause (2) of
clause 75.
3.      The matters in respect of which provisions may be made in the rules to be framed under the proposed legislation are generally
matters of procedure of detail. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore, of a normal character.

REPORT
            The main objective of the State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Bill, 2004 is to provide self-contained statutory
provisions for regulating the use of State Emblem of India1, which is the official seal of the Government.
HISTORICAL BACKGROUND
2.0        The use of State Emblem of India hitherto is governed by the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950
(Annexure-II) and a set of executive instructions titled "Orders relating to the State Emblem of India" (Annexure-III).
2.1        The Emblem and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 is administered by Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and
Public Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs). That Act prohibits commercial exploitation of a large number of emblems and
names (both national and international) including State Emblem of India for which the prescribed maximum punishment is a meagre Rs.
5002 which hardly acts as a deterrent. Moreover, the scope of the Act is limited to the commercial exploitation of State Emblem only.
2.2        The executive instructions inter alia provide guidelines for the use of emblems in official seals, use on stationery, display on
vehicles, display on public building, use for educational purposes.
2.3        The executive instructions also mention that the State Emblem has been adopted by the Government of Assam, Bihar, Gujarat,
Maharashtra, Nagaland, Rajasthan and West Bengal. The State Emblem has been incorporated in the Emblems adopted by the
Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa, Punjab and Tamil Nadu. The
State Governments and Administrations of all Union Territories other than Chandigarh use the State Emblem.
Need for new law
2.4
               The absence of self-contained legislative framework and executive instructions having no legal enforceability has resulted in the
State Emblem been misused by organisations and individuals who are not authorised to use the same under the said instructions.
1    The State Emblem of India is an adaptation from the Sarnath Lion Capital of Asoka, which is preserved in the Sarnath Museum. The Lion Capital has four
lions mounted back to back on a circular abacus. The frieze of the abacus is adorned with sculptures in high relief of an elephant, a galloping horse, a bull and a
lion separated by intervening Dharma Chakras. The abacus rests on a bell-shaped lotus. The profile of the Lion Capital showing three lions mounted on the
abacus with a Dharma Chakra in the centre, a bull on the right and a galloping horse on the left, and outlines of Dharma Chakras on the extreme right and left
has been adopted as the State Emblem of India. The bell-shaped lotus has been omitted. The motto "Satyameva Jayate" - Truth alone triumphs-written in
Devanagari script below the profile of the Lion Capital is part of the State Emblem of India. The motto is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad (Orders Relating
to State Emblem of India, p. 1).

2.5.0          Instances of misuse of the State Emblem by private individuals/organisations/ companies/former MPs/former MLAs/retired IAS
Officers were brought to the notice of the Committee by the Ministry of Home Affairs during the presentation of Home Secretary on the
Bill.
2.5.1     The need for a self-contained legislation has therefore been felt by the Government to check improper/unauthorised use of State
Emblem by the members of public including retired Government Officials/Public servants by regulating its use by Government
functionaries.
2.5.2     A National Flag Committee constituted in October 2000 to examine various issues relating to the use/display of the National
Flag, in its report, has inter-alia  recommended for enactment of a separate legislation regulating the use of the State Emblem of India.
The recommendation was agreed to by the Cabinet in its meeting held on 15th January, 2002. Thus came the State Emblem of India
(Prohibition of Improper Use) Bill, 2004.
Objectives of the Bill
2.5.3     The proposed Bill seeks to achieve the following objectives :
                 (i)  Prohibition of misuse of State Emblem by unscrupulous members of public and by retired/former Government
officials/public servants, etc. with the intent of misleading;
                (ii)  Prohibiting the use of State Emblem for professional and commercial purposes by unscrupulous persons;
               (iii)  Regulating its use by Government functionaries;
               (iv)  Prohibition of improper use of State Emblem, which tends to create an impression that it relates to the Government;
                (v)  Prohibition of the use of State Emblem for wrongful gain i.e., for purpose of any trade, business or profession;
               (vi)  General powers of the Central Government to regulate the use of State Emblem for different purposes by authorised users
viz. State Governments, Government officials, public servants, Indian Missions, etc.;
              (vii)  Penalty prescribed for contravention of the provisions of the Bill; and
              (viii)  Power to make rules to vest with the Central Government.
SAFEGUARDS
3.0        To protect a common man from punishment/harassment for any innocuous misuse of the State Emblem, a safeguard has been
provided in the Bill to the effect that no prosecution for any offence punishable under the law shall be instituted, except with the previous
sanction of the Central Government or of any Officer authorised in this behalf by general or special orders of the Central Government.
Subordinate Legislation
3.1        The following rules regarding State Emblem are proposed to be framed under the present Bill {clause 6(2)} :–
                 (i)  Standard Design;
                (ii)  Its use as Official Seal by specified dignitaries;
               (iii)  Use on stationery by Ministers and Officers;
               (iv)  Display on vehicles;
                (v)  Display on public buildings;
               (vi)  Use on publications;
              (vii)  Use by personnel of Armed Forces/Police;
              (viii)  Use for educational purposes;
               (ix)  Use by Government officials;

3.2        The Bill in nutshell, proposes to provide legislative back up to the existing executive instructions and incorporate the portion
relating to State Emblem in the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950, in it.
PENALTIES
4.0        The penalty for unauthorised use of the State Emblem with an intent to mislead has been 
prescribed as imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend up to Rs. 5000/- or with both.
4.1        The penalty for unauthorised use of the State Emblem for commercial purposes has been prescribed as imprisonment which shall
not be less than six months but may extend to two years and with fine up to Rs. 5000/-.
VIEWS EXPRESSED DURING DELIBERATIONS IN THE COMMITTEE
5.0        A Member raised a point that the prosecuting agency to initiate the proceedings in respect of violation of the provisions of the
proposed law, should be specially provided therein.
5.1        In this regard the Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs) is of the view that it is not necessary to make any
such provision for the reason that sub-section (2) of Section 4 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 provides for trial of offences under
laws other than Indian Penal Code, 1860. It has been clarified further that where the general law relating to trial of offences as embodied
in the CrPC is intended to be made applicable, it may not be necessary to make any special provisions on the prosecution agencies and
other related matters. There are number of legislative precedents of this practice. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
has been quoted as one such example.
5.2        Another Member of the Committee raised the issue of prohibition on the display of National Flag on sports gear like T-shirts,
helmets etc. by sportspersons in various national and international sports meet. 
In this context, the Member drew pointed attention of the Committee to the restrictive provisions of Explanation 4(e) of Section 2 of the
Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. He contended that the restriction imposed by the said explanation was greatly
demotivating for members of general public and sportspersons to freely use the National Flag. He also stated that display of National Flag
on sports gear, enhances the respect for the Flag and does not in any way disrespect it. He therefore strongly felt that Explanation 4(e)
under Section 2 of the Act cited above needed to be suitably amended so as to enable public in general and sportspersons in particular to
display the Tricolour on headgears, vests, T-shirts, blazers etc. in a respectful manner as is the practice in other countries of the world.
5.3        The Committee endorsed the views and suggestions of the Member and authorised the Chairperson to write to the Minister of
Home Affairs in this regard. Accordingly, the Chairperson wrote to the Union Home Minister on March 1, 2005 requesting him to
consider the suggestion of the Member as endorsed by the Standing Committee so as to bring necessary amendment to the Prevention of
Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. The Home Minister vide his letter dated March 7, 2005 has acknowledged the reference from the
Chairperson and has stated that he is having the matter looked into. The Committee is happy to note that the Prevention of Insults to
National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2005 (Annexure-IV) which seeks to amend explanation 4(e) of section 2 of the said Act, has been
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 22 August, 2005.

6.11.0   The Schedule describes the State Emblem and its design as set out in Appendices I and II.
6.11.1   The Committee was inter-alia informed that the motto "Satyameva Jayate" - Truth Alone Triumphs - written in Devanagari script
has been taken from Mundaka Upanishad and is an integral part of State Emblem.
6.11.2   In the meeting of the Committee held on 20 April, 2005, it was pointed out by some Members that certain States are using the
State Emblem of India in their own emblems in a modified way and not conforming to the design set out in the Schedule. The issue was
flagged and the Ministry of Home Affairs was asked to ascertain the position from different States and UTs and apprise it of the status by
4 May, 2005. The Committee accordingly deferred clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
6.11.3   The Ministry sought three extensions of time in succession upto 15 June, 2005 to submit the relevant information that were
granted by the Chairperson of the Committee. Finally, the Ministry submitted the desired information on 20 June, 2005.
6.11.4   The Ministry of Home Affairs while replying to the points raised in the Committee, inter-alia informed that vide  their
Memorandum No. F 24/8/49 - Public dated 23 June, 1949, it was clarified that the provincial Governments were free to adopt distinctive
seals of their own or the Government of India's seal with such modifications as they may desire. The Ministry further informed that the
States/UTs may be categorised into four parts viz. States/UTs who have adopted the State Emblem of India without any modification
3;
States/UTs who have adopted their own Emblem 4; States that have incorporated the State Emblem of India in their Emblems without
modification5; and States that have incorporated the State Emblem of India with some modification6.
6.11.5   From the replies received from the Ministry and upon scrutiny of Emblems of various States/UTs two points emerged for the
consideration of the Committee. Firstly, some of the Emblems were prima facie  not in consonance with the secular ideals of our
Constitution and secondly, what would be the position of such Emblems and the Emblems which are not consistent with the design
enumerated in the Schedule of the Bill, after the enactment of the Bill.
6.11.6   The Committee resumed clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on 30 June, 2005, wherein the aforesaid
issues regarding use of State Emblem of India by different States/UTs were brought to the notice of the Home Secretary. The Committee
suggested that the Home Secretary may like to consult the Home Minister and the concerned States/UTs and make the Governments'
view available by 8 August, 2005, so as to enable the Committee to present its Report to Parliament during the Monsoon Session. The
clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill once again remained inconclusive.
6.11.7   In response to the direction of the Committee, the Ministry vide their communication dated 28 July, 2005 inter-alia stated that the
matter has been considered in detail and it has been felt that since certain extremely emotive issues, particularly those relating to religion
and language are involved, the matter would require detailed deliberations with the concerned State Governments. It has, accordingly,
been decided to convene a meeting of the representatives of the concerned State Governments to discuss the objectionable features
(wherever applicable) in their Emblems. The Ministry has further stated that while it is proposed to call the said meeting shortly, it is
unlikely that the issues involved will get thrashed out in one meeting as the representatives of the State Governments may like to get back
to their respective Governments for consultation. The Ministry, therefore, has anticipated that it may take quite some time for them to
finalize its report on the various points raised by the Members of the Committee and it is expected that it would require about six months'
time to complete this exercise. The Ministry, therefore, sought six months' time from the Committee for furnishing the information
desired by it.
6.11.8   The Committee considered the matter again in its meeting held on 22 August, 2005 and was of the view that no useful purpose
would be served by keeping the Bill pending for such a long time.
6.11.9   In the light of the deliberations held on the use of State Emblem as contained in the Schedule, the Committee has flagged the
above issues and calls upon the Ministry to appropriately address its concerns articulated in paras 6.11.2 and 6.11.5 before bringing the
Bill for consideration in Parliament.
6.11.10 In regard to the Ministry's Memorandum No. F 24/8/49 - Public dated 23 June, 1949, (referred to in para 6.1.4) which was issued
prior to the adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November, 1949, and its enforcement on 26 January, 1950,
the Committee is of the view that the said Memorandum needs to be reviewed after the enactment of this Bill, so that it is in consonance
with the secular ideals enshrined in the Constitution of India.

DESCRIPTION AND DESIGN
        The State Emblem of India is an adaptation from the Sarnath Lion Capital of Asoka which is preserved in the Sarnath Museum. The
Lion Capital has four lions mounted back to back on a circular abacus. The frieze of the abacus is adorned with sculptures in high relief
of an elephant, a galloping horse, a bull and a lion separated by intervening Dharma Chakras. The abacus rests on a bell-shaped lotus.

and a galloping horse on the left, and outlines of Dharma Chakras on the extreme right and left has been adopted as the State Emblem of
India. The Bell-shaped lotus has been omitted.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
        The use of State Emblem of India is presently governed by a set of executive instructions, which cover various aspects, such as,
standard design of the State Emblem of India, its adoption by the State Government, its use in the official seals and on stationery, design
of official seal, display on vehicles and on public buildings, use for educational and various other purposes, etc. However, these
instructions or orders do not have any legal sanction. The State Emblem of India being the official seal of the Government, its use on any
document or thing tends to create an impression that it is an official document or thing of the Government. Therefore, there is a need to
prevent its misuse by unauthorised persons.
2.     In order to regulate the use of State Emblem of India with a view to 
(i) prohibiting the use of the State Emblem of India by members of the public, including retired/former Government officials/public
servants, etc., unless specifically authorised by the Central Government; (ii) prohibiting the improper use of State Emblem of India for
professional and commercial purposes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto; and (iii) regulating its use by
Government functionaries, it is proposed to enact a self-contained legislation.
3.     The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

ORDERS RELATING TO THE STATE EMBLEM OF INDIA
I–STATE EMBLEM OF INDIA—DESCRIPTION AND DESIGN
(1)        The State Emblem of India is an adaptation from the Sarnath Lion Capital of Asoka which is preserved in the Sarnath Museum.
The Lion Capital has four lions mounted back to back on a circular abacus. The frieze of the abacus is adorned with sculptures in high
relief of an elephant, a galloping horse, a bull and a lion separated by intervening Dharma Chakras. The abacus rests on a bell-shaped
lotus.

            The profile of the Lion Capital showing three lions mounted on the abacus with a Dharma Chakra in the centre, a bull on the right
and a galloping horse on the left, and outlines of Dharma Chakras on the extreme right and left has been adopted as the State Emblem of
India. The bell-shaped lotus has been omitted.
            The motto "Satyameva Jayate",—Truth alone triumphs—written in Devanagari script below the profile of the Lion Capital is part
of the State Emblem of India. The motto is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad, an ancient scripture.
            NOTE : The State Emblem of India has been referred to as the State Emblem in the following paragraphs.
            (2) For the accurate reproduction of the State Emblem, two standard designs have been approved. Prints of these designs are at
Appendices I and II. Design I is in a simplified form and is intended for reproduction in small sizes such as for use in stationery, seals and
die-printing. For reproduction in bigger sizes, only design II, which is more detailed, should be used.
            All reproductions of the State Emblem should strictly conform to Design I or Design II.
            Photographic designs of the State Emblem can be obtained from the Manager, Photo Litho Wing, Government of India Press,
New Delhi.
            Samples of standard dies of the State Emblem can be obtained from the Office of the Chief Controller of Printing and Stationery,
New Delhi.
II—ADOPTION BY STATE GOVERNMENTS
            The State Emblem has been adopted by the Governments of Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Nagaland, Rajasthan and West
Bengal and has been incorporated in the Emblems adopted by the Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka, Orissa, Punjab and Tamil Nadu. The Governments and Administrations of all Union Territories other than Himachal Pradesh
and Chandigarh use the State Emblem. The Union Territory of Chandigarh has incorporated the State Emblem in the emblem adopted by
it.
III—USE IN THE OFFICIAL SEALS
            The State Emblem is the official seal of India. The use of the State Emblem for official seal is restricted to the following :
                 (i)  President;
                (ii)  Vice-President;
               (iii)  Union Ministers;
               (iv)  Ministers and other Officers of the Central Government including Diplomatic Missions abroad;
                (v)  Governors, Lieutenant Governors, Chief Commissioners and Administrators of Union Territories; and
               (vi)  Ministers and Departments and Offices of the State Governments and of Union Territory Governments and
Administrations who have adopted the State Emblem.
            Offices of Central Government permitted to use distinct emblems of their own may, however, use the same in their seals.
IV—USE ON STATIONERY
            (1) The State Emblem when printed or embossed on demi-official stationery used by Ministers and Officers should appear on the
top left hand corner. The lettering like "Home Minister" or "Ministry of Home Affairs" should appear on the top right hand corner.
            (2) The demi-official stationery used by Ministers should be embossed or printed in blue.
            (3) The demi-official stationery used by officers should be embossed or printed in red colour except where an officer is
specifically authorised to use such stationery in some other colour. Names of officers should not be printed on such stationery.

purpose in the case of the Members of the Lok Sabha is green and that in the case of the Members of the Rajya Sabha is red. Such
stationery, when supplied by the Chief Controller of Printing and Stationery, does not contain the names or addresses of the Members.
But the Members may, at their discretion get such stationery, with their names and addresses, printed at private presses approved for this
purpose by the Government of India in the Ministry of Urban Development.

BILL
further to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.
           BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifty-sixth Year of the
Republic of India as follows :–
 
             1. This Act may be called the Prevention of Insults to
National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2005.
Short title.
         2. In the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971,
in section 2, in Explanation 4, for clause (e), the following clause
shall be substituted, namely :—
        "(e) Using the Indian National Flag,–
                (i) as a portion of costume, uniform or accessory of any
description which is worn below the waist of any person; or
                        (ii) by embroidering or printing it on cushions,
handkerchiefs, napkins, undergarments or any dress material; or".
Amendment of
section 2 of Act 69 of
1971.
 
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
        Section 2 of the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, inter alia , provides punishment for disrespect to the National
Flag. One of the actions that constitutes disrespect to the National Flag is using the National Flag as a portion of costume or uniform of
any description or embroidering or printing it on cushions, handkerchiefs, napkins or any dress material.
2.     There were demands from the common citizens in general, and the sportspersons in particular, to express their love and affection for
the National Flag by displaying it on their dresses, headgear, T-shirts, vests, etc., in a respectable manner. The Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs was also of the view that the restrictions imposed by Explanation 4(e) of section 2
of the said Act are demotivating the general public and sportspersons.
3.     In view of the above, it is proposed to amend the said Explanation of section 2 of the said Act, which will enable the members of the
public to use the National Flag on their costumes, uniform or accessory of any description in a respectable manner with the safeguard that
the National Flag shall not be used as a portion of costumes, uniform or accessory of any description worn below the waist, nor it would
be used by way of embroidering or printing in items of daily use such as cushions, handkerchiefs, napkins, undergarments or any dress
material.
4.     The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.
SHIVRAJ V. PATIL
  NEW DELHI;
The 10th August, 2005.

Report
The subject matter of grievances of the Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of Central Industrial Security Force (CISF)
has been engaging the attention of the Committee on Home Affairs since 1999.  The Committee first took up the issue
in its Fifty Fourth Report (1999-2000) on Demands for Grants of Ministry of Home Affairs and followed it up in Fifty
Ninth Report (2000-2001) on Demands for Grants. In its first chapter of Eighty-third Report (2001) the Committee had
extensively dealt with the problem.
1.1       The genesis of the grievances of CISF Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ officers may be traced to the year 1987 when
the post of Assistant Commandant of CISF was accorded Group ‘A’ status and selection procedure for that post was
made through Civil Services Examination (CSE) conducted by Union Public Service Commission (UPSC).  The
Assistant Commandants selected through CSE of UPSC were neither allowed to take subsequent CSE for improvement
of their career (IFS, IAS, IPS), nor were they given the benefits of organized Group ‘A’ service in their organization
(CISF) leading to acute stagnation creating resultant resentment and demoralization amongst them.  The magnitude of
the sufferings of the direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF was accentuated by the application of ROTA-QUOTA1

117th roport of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/117threport%20.htm[01-07-2016 11:33:43]
system.  The ROTA-QUOTA system followed in CISF is heavily stacked against the direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers
whose career progression is doomed right from the moment they joined  the CISF as a result of this system.  The 150
odd officers recruited between 1987-1996 through Civil Services Examination were denied the opportunity to better
their performance in the same examination, which was available to their counterparts (ACs) in CRPF, BSF & ITBP
presumably on the ground that the former were recruited through CSE and hence treated at par with their batchmates
who were allocated one of the Group ‘A’ Civil Services.  Considering the pathetic condition with regard to the career
prospects of direct recruit Group ‘A’ officers of CISF, the Committee in its Fifty-fourth Report on Demands for Grants
(1999-2000) of Ministry of Home Affairs, dwelt at length on the subject with a view to persuade the Ministry to find
some lasting solution to the problems of these officers.  Accordingly, it recommended for the reallocation of direct
recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF to Indian Police Service (IPS) or to any other Group ‘A’ Service as no other solution
was going to make any perceptible change to their position because irreparable damage had already been done to them
by the ROTA-QUOTA system.
1.2       In response to the recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its Fifty-fourth Report, the
Ministry of Home Affairs in its Action Taken Replies thereon, intimated that a Committee under the Chairmanship of
Shri Nikhil Kumar, Special Secretary (ISP) in the Ministry had been constituted to examine the service grievances of
those Officers.  Further action in the matter was proposed to be taken on the recommendations of the Committee.
2.         The Nikhil Kumar Committee which was constituted pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee
contained in its Fifty-fourth Report, made the following recommendations relating to the career prospects of the Group
‘A’ Officers of the CISF:
(i)         The promotion quota for cadre officers in the rank of Commandant (both Junior and Sr. Commandants) may be
increased to eighty per cent while the deputation quota for the IPS officers be restricted to twenty per cent;
Promotion quota for cadre officers of CISF at the rank of DIG may be increased to sixty per cent and the quota for IPS
officers may be reduced to forty per cent.  The quota at the level of IG may be retained at 33.3 per cent;
Rules relating to maintenance of seniority may be amended.  All directly recruited officers of one batch should be
placed in a bunch, above the promotee officers of the same year.  The year of declaration of result of the relevant Civil
Services Examination should be taken as the seniority year for the directly recruited officers as is done in case of All
India Services;
Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF may be nominated for deputation to other forces and organizations so that the prevailing
stagnation is removed; and
It did not find it feasible to reallocate the directly recruited Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF to IPS and other Group ‘A’
Services.
2.1       The Ministry expressed its inability to abolish the ROTA-QUOTA system and felt that even if that system were
to be abolished, it could only be done prospectively which was not going to benefit the aggrieved officers. No
substantial improvement in the service conditions could be noticed with the limited implementation of some of the
recommendations of the Nikhil Kumar Committee by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2.2       The Committee again considered the grievances of those officers during the examination of Demands for Grants
(2000-01) of Ministry of Home Affairs and reiterated, in its Fifty-ninth Report, its earlier recommendation as contained
in its Fifty-fourth Report that direct recruit Group ‘A’ officers of CISF who had been recruited through Civil Services
Examination should be reallocated to IPS or to any other Group ‘A’ Civil Service to redress their grievances.
2.3       In the meantime a delegation of the direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF met the then Home Minister twice
- on 24 April and 24 July 2000 regarding redressal of their grievances. 
2.4       The Ministry of Home Affairs in its ATR on Fifty-ninth Report of the Committee stated that by 31 December
2000 a final decision on the issues relating to grievances of these officers would be taken.  The Ministry sought two
subsequent extensions for submission of final reply in the matter but could not arrive at the final decision on the issue. 
While seeking second extension the Ministry informed that a Departmental Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri
A. K. Bhandari, Special Secretary (JKA) had been constituted to look into the grievances of Group ‘A’ officers of the
CISF & other CPMFs and to examine the recruitment patterns in the past and suggest measures to remove any future
bottlenecks in the promotions of the cadre officers of the Para-Military Forces;
2.5       The Bhandari Committee, inter alia, recommended cadre review of the CPMFs; grant of Junior Administrative
Grade/Senior Administrative Grade as time scales; adoption of uniform system of seniority in all the CPMFs; doing
away with Rota-quota system; relaxation in residency period for promotions; deputation of those officers in larger
number to Intelligence Bureau (IB), Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), State Police Forces, PSUs, etc.
2.6       The Ministry had stated that in pursuance of the recommendations of the Bhandari Committee following actions
had been taken by the Government:

117th roport of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/117threport%20.htm[01-07-2016 11:33:43]
Recruitment of Asstt. Commandants in CISF had been delinked from CSE from 2003 onwards in order to remove the
confusion created due to their recruitment through the Civil Services Examination.
After consulting Ministry of Law, draft Seniority Rules have been referred to DOP&T in order to remove the
contentious issue of Rota-Quota system of fixation of seniority.
Senior Time Scale (Rs.10,000-15,200) had been granted to Asstt. Commandants of CPFs on completion of 4 years
service in the grade.
For promotion to various ranks, residency period prescribed in Recruitment Rules had been reduced upto one year in
relaxation of the prescribed norms.
Deputation policy had been relaxed and liberalized for direct recruit officers.  Their names were being forwarded for
deputation to other Departments/PSUs even when they had not completed the prescribed 10 years of service in the
Force.
2.7       The Committee has however noted that none of the recommendations have been fully implemented till date. In
reality, none of those measures of the Government has brought in any substantial improvement in the career prospects of
direct recruit Group 'A' Officers of CISF recruited between 1987-1996 through CSE.
3.         Keeping in view the cavalier manner in which the Ministry of Home Affairs had handled the whole issue, as also
its repeated attempts to furnish wrong information thereby misleading the Committee, the then Chairman of the
Committee wrote to the then Home Minister on December 4, 2000 (Annexure-I) and the latter responded to the issues
raised (Annexure-II). The then Home Minister had assured (Annexure-III) the then Chairman of the Committee on
Home Affairs that the Bhandari Committee recommendations would be finally implemented within next six months
which would bring desired benefits to the direct recruit Group 'A' Officers.
3.1       In view of the continued dithering and adoption of dilatory tactics on the part of Ministry of Home Affairs, the
Committee decided to present a separate report on the issue covering all aspects and accordingly came out with its
Eighty-third Report (Chapter-I). In that Report, the Committee observed that direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF
should not be made to pay for the wrongs of the decision makers who failed to foresee the negative fallout of their
dispensation and reiterated its earlier recommendation as contained in its Fifty-fourth and Fifty-ninth Reports that those
officers be reallocated to IPS or any other Group ‘A’ Civil Service. 
3.2       Further, as a temporary measure before arriving at a final decision on the issue, the Committee recommended
that the Ministry of Home Affairs should adopt a liberal deputation policy vis-à-vis those officers so that some interim
relief was provided to them till a lasting solution was found to their grievances.  The Committee also sought a quarterly
report on this issue so as to know the number of officers actually sponsored and released for deputation.
3.3       The Eighty-third Report was presented to both Houses of Parliament on 19 December 2001.  The ATR on the
recommendations contained in the Report were received in the Secretariat from the Ministry on 18 March 2002. 
4.0       The oral evidence of the Home Secretary on the issues arising out of the ATRs furnished by the Ministry was
heard in the meeting of the Committee held on 12 November 2002.  The Home Secretary in that meeting had assured
that the issue would be settled one way or the other within three months.  The deadline set by the Home Secretary
expired on 11 February 2003. 
4.1       In the meantime, the Ministry was requested to furnish replies/comments on (i)   questionnaire prepared by the
Secretariat based on points/issues arising out of the ATRs; and (ii) statement containing the remarks of the Secretariat
on the ATRs, as approved by the Committee, by 22 November 2002.   These remarks, inter alia, contained suggestions
for reallocation of direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF either to Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) by
restructuring it or to an organised vigilance set up or to the security set up of Indian Embassies. The Ministry of Home
Affairs through their communication dated 27 November 2002 requested for an extension of fifteen days to furnish the
requisite replies.   However, nothing was heard from the Ministry and after a lapse of nearly three months, the Ministry
sent a communication dated 20 February 2003 (Annexure-IV) stating that the comments of the Ministry on the remarks
of the Secretariat were being finalized in consultation with Department of Personnel & Training (DOPT) and the CISF,
which would be sent by 30 June 2003.
4.2       Finally, the replies/comments of the Ministry of Home Affairs were submitted, in summary form, by the then
Home Secretary vide his D.O. letter No.45019/6/2002/Pers.(Vol.II) dated 20 June 2003 addressed to the then Chairman,
Committee on Home Affairs (Annexure-V) and in detailed form, by the Ministry vide its letter No.45019/6/2002 Pers.
(Vol.II) on 20 June, 2003.  The Ministry rejected almost all the recommendations/suggestions of the Committee. 
However, the letter from the Home Secretary addressed to the Chairman, Committee on Home Affairs stated that the
suggestion of reallocation of these Officers to CBI, CVC or Foreign Missions abroad was not acceptable to the
concerned organizations and Ministry of Home Affairs as the organizational structure was decided on the basis of its
requirement; hence the solution seemed to lie within the CISF only.  He further assured the Committee that a

117th roport of committee on Home Affairs

restructuring proposal had, therefore, been envisaged suggesting creation of a number of higher-level posts which would
provide more avenues of promotion at higher levels to the Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF.
5.         Due to dissolution of the Thirteenth  Lok Sabha on 6 February 2004, the Committee’s tenure came to an end
and, therefore, it could not consider the subject further.        
6.         However, on the eve of the constitution of the new Committee, the Committee Secretariat requested the Ministry
on10 June 2004 to furnish the updated replies/comments on the observation of this Secretariat on the ATRs by 30 June
2004 so as to enable it to place the same before the newly constituted Committee.
7.0       The Ministry, however, sought further extension of three months upto 30 September 2004, which was not
acceded to by the Secretariat and the Ministry was directed by the new Committee to furnish the same positively by 16
August 2004.
7.1         The Ministry vide letter No.45019/6/2002-Pers.1 (Vol.II) dated 6 September 2004 furnished the updated
version of the replies.         (Annexure-VI).  Actually the latest ATR furnished by the Ministry of Home Affairs was
reiteration of its earlier replies by not accepting the recommendation of the Committee for reallocation to  IPS or any
other Group ‘A’ Civil Service to the aggrieved CISF Group A Officer directly recruited through CSE.
7.2       In the final analysis, it may be observed that despite persistent efforts made by the Committee on Home Affairs
to impress upon the Ministry of Home Affairs the need to find a just and lasting solution to the grievances of direct
recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF, things remain more or less the same as they were when the Committee first took up
this issue six years ago.  Though the Ministry of Home Affairs has claimed to have taken several steps to improve the
service conditions of these officers, the avowed steps are more cosmetic in nature than of any substance.  In view of the
steps taken by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Committee posed the following questions to the Ministry of Home
Affairs and Department of Personnel and Training:
Whether sufficient avenues have been created within CISF to ensure that a direct recruit officer reaches Senior
Administrative Grade (SAG)/IG level after rendering 20-24 years of service.  If not, what is the utility of having a cadre
review or restructuring?
How the proposed cadre restructuring would benefit the direct recruit Group 'A' officers of CISF recruited between
1987-1996?
The benefit of financial upgradation has been given only at the Senior Time Scale level after completion of four years in
service.  If the Ministry considers ‘financial upgradation’ as the second best alternative to functional promotion then
why it does not extend the same benefit to the next higher levels i.e. JAG, SAG, etc. also?
Whether the steps taken so far by the Ministry are adequate enough to address the problems of these officers in their
entirety?  If not, how does it propose to address the long pending grievances of these officers with a view to find lasting
solutions to them?
Whether the Ministry has implemented the recommendations of Bhandari Committee in toto?  If not, reasons thereof.
If the Ministry of Home Affairs is adopting a liberal deputation policy vis-à-vis direct recruit officers then why is it so
that only a small number of officers have been allowed to go on deputation?
The Ministry has reversed the earlier recruitment policy of Asstt. Commandants of CISF and since 2003 their
recruitment has been combined with the CPO Examination conducted by UPSC.  Whether the Ministry has
contemplated any special dispensation for the Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers, recruited between 1987-1996 through
CSE which is now a moribund cadre?
The Ministry has turned down the repeated recommendation of the Committee for reallocation of Direct Recruit
Officers to IPS or another Group ‘A’ Service, on the ground inter alia that such a step might lead to number of such
demands from other services.  However, the fact is that no other civil service has become a dead cadre like the Group
‘A’ Officers of CISF.  Whether the Ministry would reconsider its decision to ameliorate the suffering of the direct
recruit officers?
7.3       The Ministry, while furnishing its replies to the questions posed by the Committee, has stated that:
whereas in 1969, the strength of CISF was 3,129 only, which  increased to 94,347 at present.  Despite this increase in
the strength of the Force, no cadre review or restructuring was undertaken at HQ level.  Cadre review thus became
necessary due to enlarged role and increased manpower of the Force at lower levels.  However, creation of higher level
posts merely to grant functional promotions to officers will adversely affect the command and control structure of the
Force and is not in the interests of the organization.
 the orders on cadre restructuring have been issued on 13.12.04, creating 80 temporary Group ‘A’ posts and 175
temporary posts as supporting staff.  After the restructuring, 24, 60, 31, 19 and 4 Direct Recruit Group A Officers of
1983-1996 batches are expected to get the ranks of IG, DIG, ADIG, Sr. Commandants and Commandants, respectively.
5 Direct Recruit ACs who joined CISF service in 1996 and 2 ACs joining in 1997 have been regularly promoted as DCs

1.1.2005.
in case of All India Service Officers, including IPS Officers, service is counted from first January of the batch year for
the purpose of grant of promotion, whereas in the case of CISF officers, service is counted from the date of their joining.
while financial up-gradation may not be a substitute of functional promotion, this is nevertheless the second best
alternative given the organizational constraints.  Proposal to grant financial up-gradation in DC’s pay-scale has already
been agreed to and implemented in all the CPFs.
the proposal for similar financial up-gradations to JAG/SAG levels was considered by MHA in consultation with
DOP&T which did not agree to it as promotions to JAG level and above are supposed to be earned.  DOP&T however
suggested to take it up again when revised strengths at various levels in all the CPFs is known after their restructuring.
further action is being taken to fill up the additional Group A posts sanctioned after restructuring of the Force.  This will
provide them more avenues of promotion.
from the date of oral evidence of Home Secretary before the Committee on 10.4.2001, the Government have been
liberally nominating CISF Group A officers for deputation to other organizations. At present there are eight direct
recruit group A officers (CSE 1987-96) on deputation. Even after their selection on deputation, some officers (42)
refused to go on deputation to organizations like State Police, IB, SPG & NSG.  On selection, some of these officers put
down certain conditions for their deputation to these organizations which were not acceptable to the latter.  Hence, they
could not join on deputation even after being selected.
the demand of the CISF Group A Officers is that seniority principles as are applicable to the All India Services, where
direct recruits of a particular batch/recruitment year are placed en-bloc senior to the promotee officers who are promoted
in that recruitment year against the promotion quota, should be adopted in their case.  This has been considered by
MHA in consultation with the DOP&T, but has not been agreed to as the CPFs, including CISF, are not comparable
with the All India Services,  As in the case of other central government employees and services, the general principles
of seniority as per the rota-quota system should be applied by all the other services/posts, including those in CISF.
CISF is a need based Force and its structure is more horizontal than being a typically vertical pyramid.  Rota quota
system of seniority as applied to all posts in the CISF is not a stumbling block in the career prospects of its officers. 
However, the abolition of Rota-quota system if & when effected cannot be applied retrospectively to the benefit of
already recruited Group A direct officers.
due to recruitment of Assistant Commandants through a separate examination by the UPSC, the existing direct recruit
officers of CISF are not affected.  However, MHA have been taking all possible steps to improve their career prospects
within the organizational constraints.  In the recent restructuring of the Force, a number of higher posts upto IG level
have been created, which will further improve their promotional prospects.
After the restructuring of the CISF, a number of higher level posts of DC, Commandant/Sr. Commandant, ADIG, DIG
and IG have been created which will further improve their promotional prospects.  Career-wise, officers of CISF are not
in disadvantageous position when compared with similarly placed officers of the Central Police Forces under MHA.
8.0       The Committee was not satisfied with the Action Taken Replies furnished by the Ministry and updated replies
sent to the Committee subsequently. The Committee has repeatedly articulated its concern over the fact that promotion
prospects for those officers had been completely blocked and they did not get parity either with other Group ‘A’ Civil
Services or with other Central Para-Military Forces which ought to have been done.  The impugned rules of the Civil
Services Examination which barred the direct recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF from joining an All India Service or
availing further chances in the examination to improve their ranking on the ground that all Group ‘A’ Services were at
par, were not enforced in case of other services including the CPMFs personnel.
8.1       During the evidence of the  Home Secretary before the Committee on 25 February 2005, it was  conveyed to him
that the grievances of Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF had been engaging the attention of the Standing
Committee for the past six years during which successive Committees had examined the matter in detail and presented
their Reports to Parliament containing views, observations and recommendations on the subject.  It was also stated that
each predecessor Committee had come to the conclusion that injustice had been done to the Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ of
CISF officers of 1987-1996 batches and had strongly recommended that steps ought to be taken and action initiated to
redress the grievances of those officers.  The Committee was not satisfied with the Action Taken Replies furnished by
the Ministry and updated replies sent to the Committee subsequently.  The Members felt that the Committee had
repeatedly articulated its concern over the fact that promotion prospects for those officers had been completely blocked
and they did not get parity either with other Group ‘A’ Civil Services or with other Central Para-military Forces which
ought to have been done.  It was observed that the impugned rules of the Civil Services Examination which barred the
Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF from joining an All India Service or availing further chances in the

117th roport of committee on Home Affairs

examination to improve their ranking on the ground that all Group ‘A’ Services were at par, were not enforced in case
of other services including the CPMFs personnel.
8.2       The Home Secretary responded to the observations of the Committee and stated that he did get the feeling that
perhaps the Home Ministry had not been able to meet the expectations of the Committee in the matter.  The Home
Secretary inter alia highlighted what had been done by the Ministry in the meantime.  He made a distinction between an
organized civil service and a uniformed police force.  He then stated that as the CISF was a uniformed police force,
there was an inbuilt resistance in its very structure towards creating too many posts at the higher level which was also
true for the other CPMFs and the Armed Forces.  The Home Secretary stated that it was not in order to draw
comparisons between Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF and the IPS, as the structure of the latter was different. 
He informed the Committee that the Ministry had tried with the lateral shifting of those personnel of CISF to other
forces or to other organizations but the same did not succeed.  The number of persons who had been adjusted in that
manner had not been enough to make any major difference to the promotion prospects of the CISF which was the
concern of the Committee.  So the problem before the Ministry was how to redress their grievances within the
constraints.  In the same genre he admitted that although certain decisions had been taken on the basis of the
recommendations of the Nikhil Kumar Committee and Bhandari Committee, they did not make any substantial
difference in the career prospects of the CISF Officers.  Therefore, the Ministry fell back on the age-old methodology of
improving the service conditions by creating higher level posts.  He added that because of the cadre restructuring of the
CISF, most of the Direct Recruit personnel of CISF, recruited between 1987-96 would have a better chance to reach up
to the level of IG.
8.3       Thereupon it was pointed out that the most important recommendation of the Nikhil Kumar and the Bhandari
Committees was the abolition of rota-quota system which Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions had
not agreed.  In this context, the reasons for rejecting the said recommendation was enquired from the Secretary
(Personnel).  
8.4       Secretary (Personnel) replied that the CISF had not yet been constituted as a Group ‘A’ Service of the
Government of India and the demand of the Direct Recruit officers that they should be treated at par with All India
Services was untenable.  As regards the recommendation for abolition of rota-quota system, Secretary (Personnel) stated
that it was structurally unacceptable at that moment.  Besides, there would be objections from the promotee officers
because the rota-quota system was giving them a position which a Direct Recruit wants and its abolition would be quite
harmful to the interests of the promotees themselves.  Secretary (Personnel) felt that it was a matter which the Home
Ministry would have to deliberate within themselves and as far as the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions was concerned, its view was quite clear that the rota-quota system would be inapplicable only when the CISF
was constituted as a Group ‘A” service which at that moment it was not.
8.5       Thereupon, it was observed that while debarring the candidates, who got selected as Assistant Commandants in
CISF through Civil Services Examination, from taking further chances for improving their ranks, the Ministry
somewhere sought to create an impression that the post of Assistant Commandant in CISF was a Group ‘A’ Service and
as all Group ‘A’ Services were at par. As it was an extraordinary situation, the whole Committee was concerned over it
and was very keen to find a just and lasting solution to the satisfaction of all concerned.  The Committee was once again
convinced that injustice had been done to the 150 and odd Assistant Commandants recruited through the Civil Services
Examinations between 1987-96.
8.6       While responding to the statement of the Home Secretary that cadre restructuring would bring lot of
improvement in their career prospects, the Committee felt that it would benefit only 0.2 per cent of the affected officers
and that their share of benefit out of the cadre restructuring would only be peanuts.  The Committee observed that unless
and until the Government gets those officers absorbed in other services/organizations, their problem would not be
solved, as there was no possibility of redressal of their grievance within the CISF.  In that context it was stated that
when a large number of vacancies were available in various organizations, the Ministry should try to adjust the affected
officers against those posts.  Alternatively, the Ministry could permanently earmark the required number of posts for
those officers to be filled up by deputation.  In short the Committee urged upon the Government to come out with some
solution so that justice could be done to the aggrieved officers of the 1987-96 batches. It was also suggested to the
Ministry to stop inducting officers on deputation into CISF so that those posts could be offered to the Direct Recruit
Assistant Commandants.
8.7       Thereafter DG, CISF apprised the Committee of the status of implementation of recommendations of the Nikhil
Kumar Committee and Bhandari Committee Reports and the perceived resultant benefit to the Direct Recruit Group ‘A’
officers of CISF.  He inter alia stated that twenty four officers would reach upto the rank of IG and fifty eight officers
could go upto the rank of DIG.  He compared CISF officers’ career prospects with three best and three worst Group ‘A’

Service and stated that it was true that the career prospects of the Direct Recruit CISF officers was slightly less than that
of the three best Group ‘A’ Services whereas in relation to the three worst Group ‘A’ Services, the CISF officers’ career
prospects were better.
8.8       Thereupon, the Committee took exception to the comparison made by DG, CISF of the Direct Recruit officers of
CISF with certain Group ‘A’ Civil Services.  According to him such a comparison was unfair because a CISF personnel
was ready to sacrifice his life to protect the country’s important installations and VIPs.  Moreover, such a comparison
was also unfair in the sense that the disability that was imposed upon the Direct Recruit CISF officers in the Civil
Services Examination, was not imposed on the Group ‘A’ Civil Services with whom the DG, CISF had sought to
compare the Group ‘A’ Assistant Commandants of CISF.
8.9       Thereafter, the Committee clarified to the officers of the Ministry of Home Affairs and the CISF that the
Committee was concerned about the problems being faced by the 1987-96 batches Direct Recruit Assistant
Commandants of CISF and was deliberating as to how a solution could be found to their problems.  At this stage the
Home Secretary clarified that the Ministry had looked at every possibility and had sought to find a way out of the
impasse but acknowledged that it still did not meet the total requirement of the situation.  In that context Home
Secretary stated that if the Ministry changed a particular rule in favour of CISF Direct Recruits, then that rule would
affect others and there lied the problem of the Ministry. It was observed that though the Ministry, by delinking the
recruitment of Assistant Commandants in CISF from the Civil Services Examination and linking it with the CPOs
Examination conducted by UPSC, had set right the problem for future, the fate of 150 plus officers still hanged in the
balance. The Home Secretary stated that he would not promise that the entire problem could be solved, but the Ministry
would try and see if some ad hoc arrangement could be made only to take care of those officers without changing the
normal rules which could have an impact on other services.  The Committee appreciated the gesture of Home Secretary
and urged upon him that a report on the action taken/proposed to be taken in the light of his observations should be sent
to its Secretariat positively by 31
st March, 2005.
9.0       The Ministry of Home Affairs in its latest communication No. 45018/1/2005-Pers.-1 dated 27th May, 2005
(Annexure-VII) has submitted a statement wherein ad-hoc arrangements proposed by CISF and Ministry of Home
Affairs to take care of the grievances of Direct Recruit Group ‘A’ Officers of CISF, have been rejected by the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department of Personnel and Training) on one ground or the other.  It
may be pertinent to point out that it is not known whether the Home Ministry while formulating the ad hoc proposals
consulted the DoP&T or not.  If prior consultations took place with DoP&T, what was their stand on the proposals?  If
prior consultations did not take place then how could the Ministry of Home Affairs make formulations unilaterally
which have now been outrightly rejected by DoP&T?   Another aspect which needs to be highlighted here is that from
time to time the Committee has made suggestions/recommendations which have been summarily turned down by the
Home Ministry.  At times the Home Ministry has formulated proposals which have been rejected by DoP&T.  This time
again the DoP&T has not agreed to the ad hoc arrangements proposed by the Ministry of Home Affairs.  In these series
of rejections of recommendations/suggestions/proposals, the line of argument of Ministry of Home Affairs and DoP&T
have been more or less the same.  In the latest instance of turning down the proposals, the same trend has manifested
once again.  The present case epitomises the indifferent attitude of the Ministry of Home Affairs and DoP&T towards
the recommendations of the Committee and towards finding a solution to the problems of Direct Recruit Assistant
Commandants of CISF.  The entire episode clearly establishes the fact that neither Ministry of Home Affairs nor
DoP&T is  genuinely interested in finding a solution to the grievances of the affected batches of Assistant
Commandants in CISF, even though they are adhoc in nature, applicable only to the 1987-96 batches of Direct Recruit
Assistant Commandants of CISF.   This is further manifested by the communication of Ministry of Home Affairs dated
27 May 2005 forwarding the comments of the DoP&T on the ad hoc arrangements proposed by the former.  It is
interesting to note that the Ministry of Home Affairs has simply forwarded the response of DoP&T like a post office
without offering its comments on the subject on which the Committee has been concerned since 1999 and produced no
fewer than three reports.
9.1       The measures suggested by MHA, though did not offer a comprehensive solution to the problems but were
definitely a step in the right direction. Abolition of Rota-Quota System for 1987 to 1996 batches and consequent
retrospective revision of seniority would have given these direct CISF officers some respite within the organisation. 
9.2       It is thus evident that the DoP&T has been rejecting all the proposals mooted by the Parliamentary Committee
including those made by the Home Ministry citing antiquated rules. The DoP&T has completely overlooked the fact that
the whole problem of Direct Recruit Officers of CISF is Government’s own creation. The Committee is convinced that
parity, as demanded by the aggrieved officers of CISF, with that of other Group A Services is just and reasonable and

that the DoP&T has been seen putting impediments by way of rejecting proposals after proposals made by the
Committee & the Home Ministry.
10.       The Committee expresses its serious concern at the dilatory, dilly-dallying and  lackadaisical approach of both
the Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoP&T) on finding a lasting
solution to the grievances of Group ‘A’ Direct Recruit Officers of CISF belonging to 1987-96 batches.  The Committee
also notes with anguish the way in which both the Ministries have blatantly ignored its recommendations/observations
contained in its various Reports since 1999, when the issue was first brought before the Committee. The Committee
observes that the latest development has created an impasse.  The Standing Committee of Parliament on Home Affairs
consisting of Members of both the Houses representing various political parties/groups, has been making unanimous
recommendations since 1999 which have been shown the scant regard. This does not augur well for the Committee
system in a parliamentary democracy. The Committee, in the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case,
recommends that the plight of the 150 odd affected Group ‘A’ Direct Recruit Assistant Commandant of CISF may be
placed before the highest authority of the Government i.e. the Union Cabinet for a just and fair solution of the problem
to the satisfaction of the aggrieved officers.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and Eighteenth
Report of the Committee on the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Bill, 2005.* 
 
2.         In pursuance of sub rule (a) of Rule 273 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha
relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred** The
Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Bill, 2005 (Annexure-I), as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 13 December
2005 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.  The Chairman directed the Committee, under
sub-rule (b) of Rule 273 of the Rules of Procedure to present the Report on the Bill within three months from the date of
reference.
 
3.0       The Committee held three sittings on the Bill. In its meeting held on 19 January 2006, the Committee heard the
presentation of the Home Secretary on the Bill and held preliminary discussion thereon.
 
3.1       In its sitting held on 31 January 2006, the Committee held discussion on the Bill.  The Committee thereafter
considered the Bill clause-by-clause on 3 March 2006.
 
4.         The Committee also considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 3 March 2006 and adopted the same.
 
5.         In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill and other
material  received from the Ministry of Home Affairs and replies of the Ministry to the queries raised by the Members
on the Bill in the meetings (Annexure-III).
 
6.         For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT
The Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Bill, 2005 seeks to amend as many as seventeen Sections
(2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,13,18,21,22,23,24,26,40 and 41) of the Protection of Human Rights (PHR) Act, 1993 (Annexure-II)
and insert a new Section 40 B to that Act.
 
1.1       Amendments to twelve Sections (2,3,4,5,12,13,18,21,22,23,26 and 40B) of the Act are substantial in nature;
amendments to two Sections (10 and 40) are clarificatory in nature and the amendments to rest four Sections (6,8,24 and
41) are consequential in nature 
 
   Some of the amendments are based on the recommendations of the Advisory Committee set-up by the National
Human Rights Commission (NHRC)1
, under the Chairmanship of Justice Shri A. M. Ahmadi, former Chief Justice of
India and others have been recommended by the Inter-Ministerial Committee comprising  Ministries of Home Affairs,
Defence, External Affairs and Law.
 
1.3       Amendments proposed in the Bill may be broadly categorized into three heads (i) amendments pertaining to
National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) (ii) amendments pertaining to State Human Rights Commission (SHRC)
& (iii) amendments to the definition clause:
Amendments pertaining to NHRC
 
1.3.0    Amendment to Section 3(2)(a) proposes modification in the eligibility criteria for the appointment of
Chairperson of NHRC to enable the Union Government to consider a retired Judge of Supreme Court having a
minimum of three years of service/experience for appointment to the post. Presently only retired Chief Justice of India is
considered eligible for the post of Chairperson of NHRC as the post enjoys the status of Chief Justice of India. The
amendment has been recommended by the Inter-Ministerial Committee to make available ample choice with the Union
Government in the appointment.
 
1.3.1    Increase in deemed members of NHRC from three to four has been proposed in the amendment to Section 3(3)
in view of bifurcation of National Commission for Schedule Castes and Schedule Tribes into two separate
Commissions, one for Schedule Castes & other for Schedule Tribes.
 
1.3.2    Amendment to Section 3 (4) enables the Chairperson, in addition to the Commission, to delegate some of the
powers and function of the Commission to its Secretary-General.
 
1.3.3    Amendment is proposed to Section 12(a) to enable the NHRC to inquire into the cases of human rights violation
and abetment thereof, referred by the Court in addition to  the present system of making inquiry suo motu or on the
petition by the victim or on behalf of the victim. 
1.3.4    Section 12(c) is proposed to be amended to enable NHRC to make surprise visits to jails, which is now possible
only after giving due intimation to the concerned State Government.
 
1.3.5    A new sub-section (6) is proposed to be added to Section 13 to enable the NHRC to transfer cases to SHRC
when NHRC feels that the complaint falls within the jurisdiction of SHRC.
 
1.3.6    Section 18 is proposed to be amended to enable NHRC to recommend award of compensation or interim relief to
the victim(s) even during the inquiry which at present can be done only after the completion of inquiry.
 
1.3.7    Tendering of resignation by  Chairperson and Members of NHRC to the President is proposed in the amendment
to Section 5 of the Act as existing provisions in the Act mention about removal only and are silent about resignation.
 
Amendments pertaining to SHRC

1.3.8    Eligibility criteria for the appointment to the post of Chairperson and Members of SHRC have been proposed to
be modified in the amendment to Section 21 (2). Only retired Chief Justice of a High Court of that State and also having
knowledge of language of that state is considered for appointment to the post of Chairperson  of SHRC. A retired Judge
of a High Court having minimum five years experience would now be considered for the post.   The amendment is
proposed as a number of States are finding difficulty to appoint Chairperson of SHRC due to lack of Chief Justice of
High Court having knowledge of vernacular of the State.  As per the proposed amendment, a Judge of High Court or
District Judge having seven years experience would be considered for appointment to the post of member of SHRC.
Furthermore, Section 21 (2) is proposed to be amended to facilitate reduction in the size of SHRC from five to three to
reduce financial burden on the State Exchequer which is illustrated in the table given below:-

1.3.9    Section 21 is proposed to be amended also to provide for the appointment of common Chairperson/Member of
SHRC for two or more States (particularly smaller and financially weaker States).  This would be useful to the smaller
states particularly in the North East who for financial or other reasons may not be in a position to establish a separate
commission.
 
1.3.10  Section 23 is proposed to be amended to provide for the resignation of Chairperson and Members to be tendered
to the Governor, as the present provision mentions removal only and is silent about resignation.
Amendment to definition clause.
 
1.3.11  The definition of the term “International Covenants” is proposed to be broadened so as to include other
conventions/covenants of General Assembly of United Nations, which the Union Government may specify by
notification, in addition to Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and Economic, Social and Cultural Rights adopted by
General Assembly.  
 
Views of Members of the Committee and Response of the Ministry of Home Affairs thereon.
 
2.0       The Home Secretary in his deposition inter alia stated that only a few recommendations of the Advisory
Committee, Chaired by Justice Ahmadi, for amendments to the principal Act, have been accepted by the Government. 
In this context, the Committee sought reasons for non-acceptance of the other recommendations of the Advisory
Committee.  It was then clarified that the Advisory Committee constituted by the NHRC had submitted its report to the
latter and not to the Government of India.  A statement (Annexure-III) showing the recommendations of the NHRC
which have not been accepted by the Government along with reasons thereof was then furnished by the Ministry and
circulated amongst the Members of the Committee. 
2.1       As per the Principal Act, only the Commission is empowered to delegate some of its powers to its Chief
Executive Officer having the designation of Secretary-General.  One of the proposed amendments is going to empower
the Chairman of the Commission also to delegate the power of the Commission to its Secretary-General.  The
Committee understood that essential functions of the Commission which were quasi-Judicial in nature could not be
delegated even by the Commission to its Secretary General.  It felt that there may be scope of misuse of power by the
Chairperson in making excessive delegation of powers to its Secretary-General by-passing other Members of the
Commission. However, the Ministry of Home Affairs in its written submission has stated that the proposed amendment

118th Report of Committe on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/ha/118threport.htm[01-07-2016 11:33:44]
is necessary to facilitate smooth functioning of the Commission. The representatives of the Ministry in the oral
submission also clarified in the meeting of the Committee held on 3 March, 2006 that the NHRC does not perform 
judicial function and the intention was only to delegate  the administrative functions and powers. The Committee,
however, desired that some safeguards may be provided in the Bill.
  The Principal Act provides for Selection Committee2
 for appointment of Chairperson and Members of NHRC and
SHRC under Sections 4 (1) and 22 (1), respectively. As per the provision of Clause 4 of the Bill, the appointment of
Chairperson/Members of the Commission would not be invalid due to vacancy or absence in the Selection Committee. 
The Committee observed that absence due to illness, out of station engagement and other such unavoidable reasons may
be considered as valid grounds. But the Bill was silent on absence of Members due to protest or dissent on the
appointment of a Chairperson or a Member. 
 
2.3       Clause 12 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 21(6) of the Principal Act to provide for common
Chairperson/Members in the State Human Rights Commission, for two or more States.  The Committee agreed that it
would be useful to smaller states, particularly NE states which may not be in a position to establish a separate
Commission.  The Committee, however, felt that the power to opt for common SHRC (Chairperson/Members(s) may be
left to the Selection Committee rather than the State Government. 
 
Clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill
 
3.0       The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its sitting held on 3 March 2006. 
Clause 2
 
3.1.0    The clause seeks to redefine International Covenants, Members of National Human Rights Commission & State
Human Rights Commission and define National Commissions for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
           
3.1.1    The clause is adopted without any change.        
Clause  3
 
3.2.0    Sub-clause (a) provides for amendment to sub-section (2) of Section 3 of the principal Act.  In sub-section (2)
the words “Chief Justice of the Supreme Court’ are proposed to be substituted by the words “a Chief Justice of the
Supreme Court or a Judge of the Supreme Court for at least three years”. The Committee noted that the Constitution
uses  the expression “Chief Justice of India”.  The Committee therefore, recommends that in the proposed amendment,
the words “Chief Justice of the Supreme Court” may be substituted by the words “Chief Justice of India”. 
 
3.2.1    The clause further proposes to amend Section 3 (3) of the principal Act in order to enable the Chairpersons of
the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes to be deemed Members
of the NHRC. The clause furthermore seeks to amend Section 3(4) of the principal Act so as to empower the
Chairperson of the NHRC to delegate some powers and functions of the Commission to its Secretary General, who is
the Chief Executive Officer of the Commission, in addition to NHRC.
           
3.2.2    The Committee is of the view that an express provision needs to be incorporated in the amendment to clear the
apprehensions and doubts that the Chairperson may tend to misuse the power in making excessive delegation.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that in sub-section (4) of Section 3 of the Principal Act, the words “except judicial

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to
submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One-Hundred and Nineteenth Report on the Demands for Grants (2006-2007) relating to the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
2.         Under Rule 272 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States, during the Budget Session after the general discussion
on the Budget in the Houses is over and the Houses are adjourned for a fixed period, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees are
mandated to consider the Demands for Grants of the related Ministries during the said recess period of Parliament and make reports thereon to the Houses
within the specific period.  But in view of the rescheduling of the Budget Session (2006), a decision was taken to conclude the entire financial business
before the Houses adjourned for the Budget recess and Rule 272 was suspended in its application to consideration of Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the
related Ministries/Departments by Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, by a Motion moved by the Minister of State in the Ministry of
Parliamentary Affairs in the Rajya Sabha on March 18, 2006 which was adopted by the House on the same day.  Notwithstanding discussion and voting
on the Demands for Grants of the respective Ministries/Departments for the year 2006-07 by the Lok Sabha, during the first part of the Budget Session, it
was decided by the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha that the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees
will examine the Demands for Grants and present their reports thereon to the respective Houses.
