CHAPTER-III
TSUNAMI-REHABILITATION AND RECONSTRUCTION
Andaman and Nicobar Islands
16. The massive earthquake and resultant tsunami, which occurred on 26.12.2004, caused
unprecedented damage to life and property. Extensive damage was reported from Car Nicobar,
Katchal, Chowra, Nancowry, Great Nicobar, etc., in the Nicobar District and Netaji Nagar and Hut
Bay in Andaman District. The earthquake and Tsunami caused extensive damage in Port Blair
harbour, jetties at Aberdeen, Phoenix Bay, Junglighat and Haddo were flooded by tidal waters. In
the Islands, 3513 persons are reported to have lost their lives (including those missing and
presumed dead).
16.1 The disaster left a severe impact on livelihood. Fishermen living on the coasts lost their
boats and fishing nets. The disaster caused an enormous environmental impact which will affect
the region for many years to come. It has been reported that severe damage has been inflicted on
ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs, forests, coastal wetlands, vegetation, rock formations,
animal and plant biodiversity and groundwater. The main effect is being caused by poisoning of
the freshwater supplies and the soil by saltwater infiltration and deposit of a salt layer over arable
land. Wells that served communities were invaded by sea, sand and earth; and aquifers were
invaded through porous rock. The saline soil becomes sterile, and it is difficult and costly to
restore the same for agriculture. It may also cause the death of plants and important soil
micro-orgarnisms.
16.2 The Committee, during its visit to Andaman and Nicobar Islands, made a study of the
impact of tsunami tidal waves on Andaman and Nicobar Islands and held discussions with a cross-
section of the people. The Member of Parliament representing the Union Territory stated that the
effect of tsunami was enormous and about 10,000 houses were to be constructed but the various
restrictions regarding forest conservation were an impediment in the rehabilitation work for
construction of permanent houses. He pleaded for payment of cash instead of built-up houses for
them. Further, he stated that Government should provide interest free loans for development of
trade and commerce which was totally ruined. Augmentation of helicopter service in view of
the strategic position of the Islands was also sought by him. He was of the view that
timely disbursement of compensation was very vital for building people’s confidence in the
Government.
16.3 The representatives of Tsunami affected people were of the view that interest free housing
loan should be provided to them. Every affected family should be provided with at least one
Government job. Compensation should be granted to the next of kin of those who had died as was
given to the victims of avalanche disaster in J&K.
16.4 The Committee. also visited the Tsunami affected villages (Tamaloo and Chuk Chuka) of
Car Nicobar to see the intermediate shelters and interacted with the people and their representatives
called Captains, Vice-Captains. They expressed reservations about the permanent shelters proposed.
to be built of concrete and steel. They wanted construction of permanent shelters with local
materials which could be expanded later on for accommodating more members of their families.
Since iron is prone to rust due to salinity it was told to be unfit for rehabilitation units.

20
17. Explaining about the damage to the agricultural land due to tsunami, the Development
Commissioner stated that the total area damaged was 10837 hectares out of which paddy and other
field crops were on 1730 hectares whereas plantation crops were on 9107 hectares. The total area
under submergence was 4339 hectares comprising paddy and other field crops. The total
reclaimable area was 6561 hectares which consisted of 694 hectares of paddy and other field crops
and 5867 hectares of plantation crops. He mentioned that a total number of 6020 farmers were
affected out of which 1743 were in Andaman district and 4277 in Nicobar district. The total
financial loss was to the tune of Rs. 321 crore. The Commissioner mentioned that out of a total
livestock/poultry of 10,85,739 in the Islands before Tsunami, 1,57,577 livestock/poultry were lost
due to tsunami for which Rs. 11.83 crore as compensation was sanctioned by Government of
India.
Rehabilitation and Reconstruction
18. Explaining about the rehabilitation efforts made, the Ministry of Home Affairs, in their
written note, stated that the Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package, announced immediately after the Tsunami,
had an outlay of Rs. 821.88 crore. Out of the outlay of Rs. 821.88 crore for immediate relief and
rehabilitation, an amount of Rs. 532 crore was sanctioned during the financial year 2005-06, out
of which an amount of Rs. 519.81 crore had been spent. Rs. 235 crore has been sanctioned for
the current year. The Ministry of Home Affairs also stated that construction of 9565 shelters was
organised for temporarily housing homeless families and these have been fully occupied. The
construction of these shelters was done in a record time of about two-and-a-half months, well
before the onset of monsoon last year.
18.1 The Government has recently approved (December, 2005) a long-term reconstruction
programme for restoring the infrastructure and livelihood in Andaman and Nicobar Islands with a
total outlay of Rs. 2677.91 crore. It is to be implemented over a period of three years. As part
of the reconstruction programme, the Government of India has approved a programme for
construction of 9714 permanent houses for the victims. The whole programme would be
implemented under the overall supervision of Ministry of Urban Development. Excavation work has
started in 20 out of 25 clusters. Construction materials have started reaching the Islands. The
target date for completion of the shelters is December, 2007, except for the shelters at Campbell
Bay which are dependent on construction of roads that are planned.
18.2 Relief for small traders and businessmen: The Ministry have also stated that revival
package for small traders and businessmen in Andaman and Nicobar Islands has been approved
under which outstanding amount in respect of loans up to Rs. 2 lakh as on 26.12.2004 will be
written off from the books of financial institutions. For loans beyond Rs. 2 lakh and up to
Rs. 5 lakh, normal interest on outstanding principal amount as on 26.12.2004 will be waived off
for three years. The total value of this package is Rs. 57.51 crore. A proposal for further
enhancing this package is under consideration.
18.3 Compensation for loss of crop:  The compensation for loss of crops was substantially
enhanced by the Government of India. As against the original rate of Rs. 4,000/- per hectare for
plantation crops, the rate has been enhanced to Rs. 90.465/- per hectare. In the case of other
agricultural crops, the rate has been enhanced from Rs. 1,000/- to Rs. 2,500/-. per hectare to
Rs. 22,231/- per hectare. The enhanced package is under implementation.
18.4 Special Package for Agriculture:  A special agricultural package of Rs. 239.54 crore under
Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package for reclaiming agricultural land that was damaged has been approved
for Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Such a package has not been approved for any other State.
Under this programme, the following activities have been undertaken:

21
➢ Repair and reconstruction of dykes;
➢ Cleaning of debris of affected areas;
➢ Application of organic manure in plantation crops area;
➢ Rainwater harvesting through construction of check dams; and
➢ Supply of pumpsets.
19. The tsunami tidal waves have caused widespread devastation in the Islands resulting
in loss of human life as well as livestock besides loss of property. The Committee feels that
considering the magnitude of destruction of life and property, whatever rehabilitation that
has been provided would not match the loss caused by the natural calamity. But the relief
provided will mitigate the suffering though the scares may not be removed permanently.
However, the Government should not leave any stone unturned to ensure early
rehabilitation of the affected people and to undertake reconstruction process to ensure that
they start their normal life at the earliest. The Committee understands that the
Government have taken up several relief measures. In regard to construction of permanent
houses, the Committee feels that the permanent shelters should be at locations which are
high on ground near the earlier habitations as the livelihood of the people requires them
to continue residing there. Similarly, while constructing the houses, use of local material
such as bamboo, wood, etc., should be preferred as they are earthquake-resistant and give
better protection from sun. The Committee also takes note of the fact that some people,
who met the Committee during its visit, desired that money may be provided to their
families so that they can construct their houses themselves. This is a better proposition
because it will engage the families in the reconstruction work till the completion of the
construction. The Government may, therefore, consider providing them financial help
besides other required material to enable the families engage themselves in the
reconstruction work.
19.1 The Committee has noted that revival package for small traders consists of waiver
of loans and interest thereon, etc. The Committee recommends that the Government may
consider increasing the package of Rs. 57.15 crore further. It also recommends that the
Government may consider providing interest-free fresh loans for at least two years to
enable them to start their business afresh. Though the Government has given compensation
for loss of agricultural crops which is now Rs. 22,231 per hectare, this is a pittance
considering the fact that agricultural land has now become saline and uncultivable and
barren. It can no longer be used for any agricultural activities and even grass will not grow.
Therefore, the Government should consider providing some package for permanent
rehabilitation of the farmers whose agricultural land is no longer useful. The package may
also contain providing assistance for business or employment.
19.2 The Committee feels that the request of the people in the islands for employment
to at least one person in each affected family needs to be considered. A one-time creation
of employment opportunities would give permanent relief to the families. Besides this,
filling up of 3000 vacant posts would also cover a large number of people. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Government may consider these proposals immediately and
take decisions thereon.
Pondicherry
20. The killer tidal waves of tsunami triggered by series of earthquakes of unprecedented scale
off the Indonesian Coast struck the coastal areas of the Union Territory of Pondicherry on the early

22
hours on 26 December, 2004. The tsunami waves hit the coasts of South India with such ferocity
and suddenness that it has turned out to be the deadliest natural disaster in the recent history,
bringing huge devastation of catastrophic proportions. Coastal fishing community and some of the
poorest people living in the coastal regions were the most affected with huge loss of lives as well
as fishing crafts and tackles and destruction of habitat and houses. Children and women were
affected most adversely as they were the least able to resist and were dragged into watery graves.
An estimated 30,000 people became homeless in the Union Territory of Pondicherry. The death toll
was 599 - 492 in Karaikal and 107 in Pondicherry.
20.1 Sixteen villages in Pondicherry and seventeen villages in Karaikal have been affected. 17,432
people in Karaikal and 26,000 people in Pondicherry have been displaced. The agricultural crop in
792 hectares of land has been damaged. Owing to the tsunami 10,061 houses were damaged.
Twenty-two relief camps were set up in Karaikal and twenty-six in Pondicherry to take care of
the relief operations of about 30,000 victims of tsunami during its peak period of functioning.
20.2 El aborating upon the relief operations, the District Commissioner, Karaikal stated that 15000
people were brought to the twenty-two relief camps within ten days of Tsunami tragedy. They
were provided with rice, kerosene and other cooking materials. NGOs also helped by way of
community kitchen. The Government also provided relief to fishermen who lost their boats
depending upon the fishing craft. The compensation of Rs. 3750/-  per hectare, as immediate relief,
was given for sea water intrusion in the agricultural fields. Another Rs 60000/-per hectare would
be given to them to take steps to restore the productivity of land. For loss of cattle also
compensation was provided on a certain yardstick. He mentioned that 1200 temporary shelters were
constructed and Rs 1000/- per family was provided for repair of houses. For constructing
permanent shelters land had been identified and required modalities were being worked out.
20.3 Reflecting upon relief and rehabilitation measures, the Relief and Rehabilitation
Commissioner stated that there were twenty-two relief centers at Karaikal and twenty-six at
Pondicherry. Ex gratia payment of Rs. 1 lakh each was made to the families of the deceased and
an amount ranging from Rs. 5000 to Rs. 4.5 lakh were given for various items such as funeral
expense, medical expense, housing subsidy for damaged houses, purchase of catamarans/boats,
wooden mechanized boats, etc. Besides this, Rs. 3750/- was also immediately given to each farmer
for damage to crops.
20.4 Rajiv Gandhi Relief Package:  The Ministry of Home Affairs have stated that immediately
after tsunami hit the coastal area of Pondicherry on 26 December, 2004, the Government of India
sanctioned an amount of Rs. 155.62 crore under the Rajiv Gandhi Rehabilitation package to the
Pondicherry Government for the purpose of immediate relief and rehabilitation measures.
20.5 Tsunami Rehabilitation Programme:  The Government has recently approved in
December, 2005, a long-term reconstruction programme for restoring the infrastructure and
livelihood in Pondicherry. This long-term reconstruction programme has a total outlay of
Rs. 518.08 crore.
20.6 Housing Reconstruction: It was further stated the Government of Pondicherry has planned
to construct 10,061 permanent houses for the victims. These will be spread over 34 settlements.
The Government of Pondicherry has formulated a Government Order governing the involvement of
the NGOs with a novel idea of insisting the NGOs to deposit 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the
project cost in any nationalised bank in the name of the NGO themselves but governed by a
tripartite agreement restricting the withdrawal of the amount by the concerned NGO after
completing 85 per cent of the work. So far, 15 MoUs have been signed with NGOs for
construction of 5,042 houses in 23 settlements. The total project cost amounts to Rs. 42.45 crore.
A total extent of 57-62-74 hectares has been acquired to facilitate construction of houses by the

23
NGOs. Out of 10,061 houses, 341 houses have already been completed and 4,827 houses are under
various stages of construction. Land acquisition is in progress for construction of remaining 4,893
houses.
20.7 Emergency Tsunami Reconstruction Project Under World Bank Aided Project:  The
Ministry have also stated that a World Bank aided project with an outlay of Rs. 158 crore for
providing permanent shelter and restoration of livelihood programme is under implementation. The
Pondicherry Government has constituted a Society namely Project Implementation Agency (PIA)
under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 to serve as an umbrella agency to implement the
assistance given by the World Bank and to undertake various other activities related thereto for
relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction in various sectors. So far the agency has taken up
construction work at 3 villages and development of infrastructural facilities in 8 villages. This apart,
the agency has taken up the work of filling up of low-lying areas where the NGOs have been
assigned with construction of houses for the affected persons.
21. The Committee notes that about 800 hectares of agricultural land as well as crops
were affected by the tidal waves in Pondicherry. Much of the land may remain permanently
unfit for farming. The relief given may not give permanent compensation to the affected
people. In all the cases of permanent loss of land, the Committee suggests that the
Government may consider raising the compensation appropriately.
21.1 After Tsunami, many farmers have been severely affected with many children getting
orphaned. Though Government has provided relief package and rehabilitation, it may also
consider providing permanent compensation in the form of reservation in employment to

21.2 In regard to construction of permanent houses, the Committee expresses its concern
that out of 10, 061 houses, only 341 houses have been completed so far and it feels that

completed within a definite time frame. Land acquisition for construction of houses may be

21.3 The World Bank aided project is an appreciable effort of the international agency.
Government may monitor the project so that targets are achieved within the given time

CHAPTER-IV
CHANDIGARH
22. The Union Territory of Chandigarh was conceived in 1949 as the capital of Punjab,
following the partition of India. The foundation stone of the city was laid in 1952 in the lap of
Shivalik hills and it was named after Goddess Chandi, whose temple “Chandi Mandir” is in its close
vicinity. A number of highly eminent and imaginative architects, both foreign and Indian were
involved in the planning of this city. Those included Charles Edouard Jeanneret also known as
Le Corbusier, a French born in Switzerland, who was instrumental in developing the Master
Plan and designing the Capital Complex. Chandigarh continued as the capital of Punjab till
1 November, 1966. Following the reorganisation of that State into Punjab and Haryana, the Union
Territory of Chandigarh was created under Section 4 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act of 1966
with its administrative functioning directly under the Central Government. The city however
continues to be the combined capital of Punjab and Haryana.
22.1 The Union Territory Administration is headed by the Administrator, who is appointed by the
President of India under Article 239(2) of the Constitution of India. The Administrator is assisted
by an Adviser. The Adviser oversees the day-to-day administration. The powers to legislate vest
with the Parliament. The nodal Ministry for the Union Territory of Chandigarh is the Ministry of
Home Affairs. Being a Union territory without a legislature, the entire plan and non-plan expenditure
is met directly from the Consolidated Fund of India. All its income goes directly to the Consolidated
Fund of India. Therefore, a single demand covering all functions of the Administration is presented
to the Parliament as part of Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
22.2 The Union Territory of Chandigarh comprises one Parliamentary Constituency and one
district. The Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC) came into existence in May, 1994 under
the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976 (as extended to Chandigarh) by an Amendment Act of
1994. An elected Mayor heads the Corporation. The Commissioner, Municipal Corporation looks
after general administration of the Corporation.
22.3 There are a number of Boards and Corporations under various Departments in Union
Territory of Chandigarh. However, two of the more important Corporations/Boards are the
Chandigarh Industrial and Tourism Development Corporation (CITCO) and Chandigarh Housing
Board (CHB) to look after the promotion of industries and tourism and housing, respectively.
Legislature for Chandigarh
23. During its visit from 13 to 14 September, 2005 to the Union Territory of Chandigarh, the
Committee was informed that the administration of the UT is very bureaucratic and not accessible
to public and there was no involvement of people’s representative due to absence of a legislature
in Pondicherry. The local Member of Parliament suggested an elected Pradesh Council and
Executive Councillors for the UT of Chandigarh instead of Legislative Assembly to solve the
problem of inaccessibility of administration.
23.1 Replying to a question as to whether the Government had ever considered/proposed to
create a Legislative Assambly for Chandigarh and whether the Government had any other proposal
such as creation of an elected body like Pradesh Council and Executive Councillors for Chandigarh,
24

25
the Ministry had informed that there was no such proposal with the Government nor had any such
proposal been considered in the recent past.
23.2 Replying to a question as to whether an Inter-State Development Council consisting of
representatives from the States of Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh and UT of Chandigarh
should be constituted for implementation of developmental projects, the Ministry had informed that
formation of an Inter-State Development Council was not considered essential after the enactment
of the Constitution (Seventy third and Seventy fourth Amendments) Acts. The urban and rural local
bodies were effectively discharging various development functions in the Union Territory. There
was also a forum, namely, the Home Minister’s Advisory Committee for Chandigarh which, inter
alia, consists of representatives from the Municipal Corporation and the Zilla Parishad, where
development issues relating to Chandigarh were deliberated upon.
23.3 The Home Secretary, during the course of his oral evidence before the Committee, stated
that they had not received any proposal for an elected body in the form of an Assembly or a
Metropolitan Council nor was any such proposal under their consideration. He also stated that the
present set up was functioning well and whatever support Chandigarh needed from the Government
of India, it was being provided, He felt that if they were able to constitute a Metropolitan Planning
Committee and strengthen and ensure that the Advisory Council to the Administrator meet more
frequently and also if the Home Minister’s Advisory Council meet regularly, there may not be a
need for alteration of the present situation. On being asked to respond to the demand of the local
MP for a Pradesh Council, the Home Secretary stated that, at present, there was no necessity for
such a political body. He further stated that it would be difficult to say, at present, as to what kind
of a political body would be there in Chandigarh in future but such a political body may not be
required right now.
23.4 The Committee notes the view of the Home Secretary that the present arrangement
is working satisfactorily. However, when the Committee visited Chandigarh, various political
leaders and general public informed that there was no forum to ventilate their grievances.
The Committee is also constrained to learn that it is very difficult for the general public
to meet the Administrator and that they felt that the present arrangement is not able to
solve their problems. The Committee is of the view that the Municipal Corporation cannot
solve all the problems of the people and the Advisory Council cannot help things to the
extent people want their aspirations to be fulfilled. Thus, there needs to be some
mechanism by which people have better access to the administration and which can address
and redress their grievances. Such mechanism, besides solving the problems of the people,
would also fulfil their aspirations. Therefore, keeping in view the aspirations of the people’s
representatives and the general public at large, the Committee recommends that some kind
of arrangement should be put in place in the UT of Chandigarh which should be
easily accessible to the public and which could effectively and adequately redress their
grievances.

therefore should have a Metropolitan Planning Committee
1 as per norms. But it was learnt that even
the District Planning Committee 2 has not yet been constituted in the UT, which may be instrumental
in preparing draft development plan for the entire district after consolidating the plans prepared by

24.1 Citing reasons for not creating the Metropolitan Planning Committee in UT of Chandigarh
so far and explaining as to how the people’s representatives are associated/involved in preparation

24.2 The Committee notes that the Metropolitan Planning Committee can go a long way
in solving the problems of the people of Chandigarh and fulfilling their aspirations. Even
though the Metropolitan Planning Committee is not the ultimate solution to the elected
legislative body, it can, to a large extent, address the problems of the masses. The
Committee suggests that suitable legislation may be brought in at the earliest so that steps
may be initiated for setting up of the Metropolitan Planning Committee.
Advisory Council to Administrator
25. There are two advisory bodies relating to Chandigarh – the Home Minister’s Advisory
Committee and the Administrator’s Advisory Council. The Ministry of Home Affairs has stated that
the Administrator’s Advisory Council was constituted on 6 January, 2005 and expanded on
20 October, 2005. The Council met on 31 January, 2005 and a few sub-groups have been
constituted. Similarly, the Home Minister’s Advisory Committee consists of the Administrator, UT
Administration, Member of Parliament from the Union Territory and members from the Municipal
Corporation, Chandigarh, including the Mayor and Zila Parishad.
25.1 The Administrator’s Advisory Council comprises the Member of Parliament; Mayor,
Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh; Chairman, Zila Parishad; three Councillors, Municipal
Corporation; one member from Zila Parishad; Presidents of various social bodies and other eminent
persons. All the national political parties have been included as members in the Council in order
to enlarge its representative character.
25.2 On the functioning and effectiveness of the Advisory Council, the Horne Secretary stated
that the Advisory Council to the Administrator should meet more frequently and needs to be
strengthened. He further apprised that the Council is not as broad-based as it should have been.
He also felt that members of the Advisory Council, should be sufficiently empowered and it be
made more broad-based. It should also meet more frequently.
25.3 The Committee understands that infrequent meetings of the Advisory Council to
Administrator might be causing problems in redressing the grievances of the people. In the
absence of a legislative body, at least, other bodies such as the Advisory Council should be
given the necessary teeth to address the people’s grievances. The Committee agrees with
the Home Secretary that the Council should meet more frequently. The Committee,
therefore, suggests that necessary steps may be taken in that direction to ensure that the
Council meet more frequently. The Committee also agrees with the view of the Home
Secretary that members of the Advisory Council should be adequately empowered. It
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take necessary steps to redefine the
powers and functions of the members of the Advisory Council and steps may also be taken
to give more powers to the Council as such. As regards the suggestion of Home Secretary
that the Council needs to be broad-based, the Committee has not received any concrete

27
proposal from the Ministry. The Committee, however, feels that the issue needs to be
deliberated upon and steps taken in this direction too.
Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh
26. The Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh came into being with effect from 24 May, 1994
after the extension of Punjab Municipal Corporation Law (Extension to Chandigarh) Act in 1994
was passed. The areas included in Municipal Corporation are:
(i) City of Chandigarh as notified by Administrator, UT of Chandigarh;
(ii) The area of erstwhile Notified Area Committee, Manimajra; and
(iii) The villages of Attawa, Badheri, Burail and Buterla.
26.1 The entire area of Municipal Corporation has been divided into 20 wards and each ward
is represented by an elected councillor. Besides this, members from amongst the persons, who are
eminent/distinguished in public life, are nominated by the Administrator, UT. Member of Parliament
from Chandigarh is an ex-officio member of the Municipal Corporation. Thus, in all there are 30
councillors, 20 elected, 9 nominated and one ex-officio. One third of total number of seats to be
filled up by direct election are reserved for women. Similarly, out of seats reserved for scheduled
castes, one third are reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes. At present 7 seats
out of 20 seats are reserved for women. Besides, out of 9 nominated members 2 are women. At
present the Corporation has 11 women councillors.
26.2 The term of the Municipal Corporation is for five years and that of Mayor, Senior Deputy
Mayor and Deputy Mayor is one year each. The office of Mayor is reserved for a women
councillor in the first and fourth year and in favour of Scheduled Caste member in the third year.
26.3 The first elected body of the Corporation came into existence on 23 December. 1996 and
completed its term on 22 December, 2001. The second term of Municipal Corporation started with
effect from 1 January, 2002.
26.4 The working of Municipal Corporation is based on the Committee system under which
various sub-committees dealing with specified subjects, such as Water supply and Sewerage,
Roads, Slum Development, Fire Services, Environment. and City Beautification, House tax etc. have
been constituted. Each of these sub-committees is headed by a chairman whereas the Finance and
Contract committee is headed by Mayor. The tenure of the Finance and Contract committee is
5 years whereas the tenure of other committees is one year. Different committees have been
delegated financial and other powers to carry on the work relating to Municipal Corporation
functions.
26.5 The main functions performed by the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh are water supply
and sewerage disposal, street lighting, sanitation, community centres, roads and bridges,
horticulture, fire services, rehabilitation of colonies/slums, whereas some regulatory functions such
as removal/prevention of encroachments on Municipal land, prevention of deposit/dumping of malba
and garbage at non-designated places, management of municipal property and management of
cremation ground are also performed by the Corporation.
26.6 The Committee during its visit also interacted with the Mayor and Councillors of Municipal
Corporation of Chandigarh. The Committee was apprised of the various initiatives taken by the
Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh viz. augmentation of water supply scheme, paid parking,
sahej safai kendras, garbage processing units, idle truck parking, multi-level parking etc. The
Committee was told that the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh is an elected body with a lot of
responsibilities but limited authority and financial resources. The Committee was apprised that the

28
decision on devolution of 17% of budget of administration of UT, as recommended by Second
Delhi Finance Commission, has not been communicated to Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh.
Besides, it was also requested to raise tax revenue to 23% in view of large scale work to be
undertaken by the Municipal Corporation.
26.7 Replying to a question about the coordination mechanism between the MCC and the
Administration, the Ministry has informed that there has been no problem of coordination between
the two. It further stated that the Municipal Corporation Act governs the relationship between the
Administration and the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh. The budget estimates prepared by the
MCC are approved by the Administration under Section 86 of the Act. Besides, as per the
provisions of Section 69 of the Act, a copy of the proceedings of the meetings of the House is
sent to the Administration by the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh. All major decisions/
directions of the Administration are brought to the notice of the House of the Corporation through
commissioner’s office.
26.7.1 On the demand of Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh for increasing the devolution of
23% tax revenue to MCC, the Ministry has stated that the National Capital Territory of Delhi has
since constituted the Third Delhi Finance Commission, vide order dated: 21.10.04 to make
recommendations on devolution of funds to local bodies for the five year period commencing from
1.4.06. Under Section 84-A(I) of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Law (Extension to Chandigarh)
Act, 1994, the Finance Commission constituted under Section 107-A of the Delhi Municipal
Corporation Act, 1957, is required to act as the Finance Commission in respect of Chandigarh also.
Chandigarh Administration vide order dated: 6-1-05 have also specified the terms of reference of
Third Delhi Finance Commission. Since the Third Delhi Finance Commission has been constituted,
the recommendations on further devolution of funds to MCC, as and. when received will be
considered for implementation the Ministry informed. It was further stated that the
recommendations of the Second Delhi Finance Commission were for devolution of 17% of the total
tax revenue to the M.C.C. which have been accepted vide letter dated 17-8-05 by the Government
of India and further steps are being taken by the administration accordingly.
26.8 While deposing before the Committee, the Administrator to the Chandigarh Administration
stated that the Administration has no problem in widening the power of MCC by transferring the
entire area of UT of Chandigarh including eighteen villages alongwith functions and funds but the
problem may arise in transferring functionaries from the Administration to Corporation. However, the
Administration has still written to the MCC for giving its opinion on transferring the eighteen villages
to MCC so that the same may be finalised and forwarded to Third Delhi Finance Commission for
appropriate recommendations. The Adviser also assured the Committee that the increase in revenue
would be commensurate to the increase of function and jurisdiction of the MCC.
26.9 The Committee is constrained to learn from the Mayor and Councillors of Municipal
Corporation of Chandigarh that it has more responsibilities with limited authority and
financial resources. The Committee has noted the MCC’s request for a share of 23 per cent
of the tax revenue. The Committee is of the view that a municipal body functions closest
to the people and needs to solve problems at the quickest possible time. For this purpose,
it requires sufficient resources. The Committee recommends that the Union Ministry of
Home Affairs may discuss the issue with the Mayor and Councillors of MCC on its
requirement of resources for a “better upkeep of the city. Steps may be taken for early
implementation of the Second Delhi Finance Commission recommendations for devolution of
17 per cent share of tax revenue until the Third Delhi Finance Commission takes a decision
on the proposed devolution of 23 per cent tax revenue.
26.10 The Committee understands that the Zila Parishad and the Panchayati Raj Institutions
(PRIs) in 18 villages would come to an end should the jurisdiction of Municipal Corporation

29
of Chandigarh be extended to these villages. And in the absence of any demand from the 18
villages for extension of jurisdiction of the MCC into their areas and the orientation of MCC
being urban, these villages may lose their rural identity without entailing any benefits and
urban taxation of the municipality may add to their woes. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the rural identity of the 18 villages may not be disturbed.
Scheduled Caste Certificates
27. The Committee during its visit learnt that scheduled castes certificates had not been issued
since 1995 without the production of residence proof prior to 1 January, 1966 (creation of UT of
Chandigarh) in the Union Territory.
27.1 In a written reply to the reasons for non-issuance of SC certificates to genuine SC
candidates after 1995, the Ministry has stated that as per guidelines dated 22.3.1977 issued by
the Government of India, a person can be issued SC certticate by the competent authority
of the State of which he or she was a permanent resident on the date of residential
Notification declaring his/her caste as SC in the State and not by the competent authority of
the State/UT to which he migrated. As the Presidential Order in respect of Chandigarh was
issued on 1.11.1966 i.e. at the time of creation of Union Territory  of Chandigarh, all the
permanent residents and their children belonging to SCs in UT Chandigarh, residing
permanently in Chandigarh are issued SC certificates. These instructions were slightly
amended by the Government of India on 17.11.1982 to the effect that the competent authority
of a State/UT may issue the SC certificate to a person who has migrated from another State
on the production of the genuine certificate issued to his/her father/mother from the State
of their origin. The SC certificates in UT are also issued accordingly to such migrant population
on production of SC certificate from the State of their origin.
27.2 Further replying as to how SC certificates were issued to the genuine SC inhabitants of
Chandigarh till 1995; the Ministry informed that except the persons who were permanent resident
of UT Chandigarh as on the date of Presidential Order dated 1.11.1966 and those who produced
the SC certificate from the State of origin, none was eligable for issuance of SC cerfificate.
However, some people other than those falling in the above two categories were issued SC
certificates inadvertently till 1995, simply on the verification of residence by the Revenue
Authorities and on production of affidavit by the applicants. Issuance of SC certificates to such
persons were inadvertent and not as per the instructions of Government of India. This practice
was discontinued in 1996 after it came to the notice of the Administration.
27.3 In response to a question regarding Government’s plan to adopt the practice of issuance of
SC certificate to bonafide SC residents in vogue in Delhi mutatis mutandis in the UT of Chandigarh;
the Ministry has stated that the problem in respect of UT of Chandigarh is peculiar as it is a newly
planned City with a sizeable migrant population. The matter is already under consideration in
consultation with the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and two meetings on 8.9.2005 and
19.10.2005 have since been held with the Ministry of Social justice and Empowerment to finalize the
issue. The Home Secretary had assured the Committee that the issue would be sorted out soon.
27.4 The Committee is constrained to note that such an important issue has been kept
unresolved for so long and the people belonging to the SC community had to suffer.  Such
issues need to be attended to without delay. The Committee trusts that Home Secretary would
stick to the assurance made before the Committee and the issue would be resolved immediately.
Career Prospects and Other Grievances of Government Teachers in the UT
28. During the visit of the Committee, a delegation of Government Teachers’ Union of the UT
met and submitted their grievances such as lack of promotional avenues for the teaching

30
community in Education Department, pending proposal regarding promotion of teachers to the post
of lecturer in Senior Secondary School in Chandigarh, deputation quota of 25% for taking lecturers
from States. The Committee was informed that some of the deputationists have got pro forma
promotion to the post of Principal in virtue of their promotion in their parent State(s) and lecturers
of the UT are working under the supervision of the deputationists who got promotion in view of
the position explained above. Demand for scrapping of the rule which allows teachers to come on
deputation from other States to the UT of Chandigarh was raised in the memoranda. Besides that,
the other issues raised in the memorandum include restoration of six weeks summer break which
is at present reduced to four weeks; change of format of Annual confidential Report (ACR);
confirmation in the post of teachers after completing three years of service; filling up of vacant
posts of teachers, introduction of Sanskrit as a subject in all Senior Secondary School alongwith
Hindi and Punjabi; restoration of the post of Director, State Institute of Education to the School
cadre; creation of post of vice-principal in all senior secondary Schools; stoppage of allotment of
houses to the persons on deputation from the States of Punjab and Haryana as these States have
their own pool of accommodations; special housing scheme by Chandigarh Housing Board for
teaching community of UT cadres.
28.1 The Committee gathers that the Chandigarh Administration is either ignorant of or
non-responsive to the problems and issues of Government Teachers. Such inept handling of
their problem would demoralise them. The Committee recommends that the problems faced
by the teachers may be addressed properly.
Air, Rail and Road Transport for Chandigarh
29. The Committee, during its visit to Chandigarh was apprised of the need for upgradation of
Chandigarh Civil Airport to International Airport as the city is the gateway to the States of Punjab,
Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. Besides, the need for electrification of
Chandigarh-Ludhiana railway line and four laning of Kalka–Chandigarh–Ludhiana highway, etc.
29.1 The Committee recommends that considering the growing importance of the
Chandigarh city, the Government should explore the possibility of upgrading the Civil Airport
to an International Airport and make it twenty-four hcurs airport, The railway service may
also be further improved keeping in view the requirement of the city and the region.
Building bye-laws
30. During the visit of the Committee, the Member of Parliament (Lok Sabha) representing
Chandigarh alleged that the indifferent attitude of the Chandigarh Administration towards the
enforcement of building bye-laws had led to alterations/additions in over ninety percent houses/flats
particularly in Phase II of the city. Issuance of notice and occasional demolitions had only added
to the woes of the people. All delegations, which met the Committee, advocated for one time
relaxation of building bye-laws to regularize the need-based alterations/additions in flats/houses.
Their views were also endorsed in the various memoranda received by the Committee during its
visit to Chandigarh.
30.1 It was alleged by the residents that the Administration adopted a very rigid and indifferent
attitude in the name of implementing building bye-laws to the alterations/additions carried out by
the house owners particularly in phase IT of the city which was creating a lot of problems for
them. It was demanded that one time relaxation in building bye-laws may be made to regularize
the need based alterations/additions in the respective flats/houses.
30.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that in order to regulate the construction in a planned
manner, certain regulations and byelaws were framed. The Administration was particular that those

31
basic requirements were adhered to. However, from time to time, various relaxations in the building
bye-laws had been made, which to some extent compromised the architectural controls and zoning
regulations.
31.0 Regarding enforcement mechanism of buildings bye-laws in the UT of Chandigarh, the
Ministry in its written reply stated that a Plan Approval Cummittee had been constituted for
sanctioning of plans which checked whether plans were in conformity with varbus building bye-
laws. Post completion stage, the enforcement is undertaken by the Estate Officer (E.O.), UT. The
competent authority (E.O.) issues notice to the persons who violate the bye-laws and the
unauthorized structure is removed following the prescribed procedure under the law.
31.1 On the issue of large scale violation of the bye-laws, the Ministry stated that violations were
largely due to the desire to maximize the built up area for various economic reasons. There are
roughly 2,00,000 dwelling units in Chandigarh whereas the enforcement staff consists of only
seven personnel. The expectation is that people will comply with the requirements of the law and
the rules. When violations come to light they are dealt with according to established legal
procedures.
31.2 On being asked whether the Government has any proposal under its consideration to give
one time relaxation in building by-laws to regularize need based alterations/addition in the flats/
houses, it was stated that a number of relaxations had already been permitted for various types of
houses/buildings through different notifications issued between the period August, 1996 to
June, 2005 and there was no other proposal under consideration.
32. The Committee feels that the situation that has arisen in Chandigarh is more or less
similar to the situation that arose in Delhi in the recent past. The Committee takes note
of the serious situation that arose in Delhi when Courts passed orders for demolition/
sealing of unauthorized constructions in Delhi leading to a public outburst as a large
number of buildings/houses were found to be affected by the said drive. Consequently, the
Central Government had to step in to prevent the situation from further worsening and
Parliament enacting a special legislation for the purpose. To avoid such a situation in
Chandigarh where too alteration/additions in houses have been made on a large scale, the
Committee feels that the Government should bring about a practical solution to the problem
by having a re-look at the building bye-laws of Chandigarh, which are quite old and also
keeping in view the needs of expanding families. Government may also in this context
consider giving a one time relaxation to the building bye-laws in Chandigarh.

32
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ADMINISTRATIVE SET-UP
The Committee is of the view that as A&N Islands, which is headed by a Lieutenant
Governor, has no public representative to supervise, to consider or to monitor the functions
of the Government apart from the Lieutenant Governor, it can at least have a Pradesh
Council. It is also of the view that Panchayati Raj cannot be a substitute for the Pradesh
Council. PRIs will look after the execution of policies and programmes under Part IX
(Article 243 G) of the Constitution, whereas the Pradesh Council would review and
supervise the functioning of the Government. (Para 3.16)
The Committee is also given to understand that there are problems of increasing
unemployment and urbanization, law and order, bootlegging. The Committee feels that these
are directly connected with development. When the State is administered by officers only,
there is no scope for monitoring and overseeing the working of. the Administration and
ultimately development is affected. When development is not taking place, people suffer
leading to increase in crime rate. These issues can be solved only by people’s participation
in governance through their elected representatives. (Para 3.17)
The Committee, during its visit to Andaman and Nicobar Islands, noted the
immensity of tsunami devastation and the problem of shortage of staff. Had there been a
Legislative Assembly the relief operation would have been addressed in a better manner.
The Committee is, therefore, of the firm view that there is a strong justification for setting
up of a Legislative Assembly for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It therefore,
recommends to the Government to take necessary steps in this direction. (Para 3. 18)
Until a final decision is taken for setting up a Legislative Asstembly, some kind of
monitoring mechanism is required. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Pradesh
Council may be revived immediately. This is all the more necessary because the
administration of the entire UT of Andaman & Nicobar Islands cannot be left to the
Panchayat Raj Institutions. These are only local self governing institutions and they cannot
be a substitute for a legislative set up. (Para 3.19)
The Committee also takes note of the fact that consequent upon the seventy third
and seventy fourth Amendments to the Constitution, though the participation of the people
in planning and execution of developmental works in the UT started at the grass-root level,
the process of delegation of powers and functions to PRIs have been very slow. The subjects
apportioned to them are limited and even in those areas the transfer has not been
complete. The Committee, therefore, recommends that local bodies may be delegated more
powers and functions without further delay so that they can meet the people’s aspirations.
Further the Committee recommends that these bodies should be supported by adequate
staff, finance and other logistics. (Para 3.20)
Sociological Set up
The Committee takes note of the fact that there are five primitive tribes in the
whole of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. They fulfil the essential characteristics of tribals.
The Committee understands the compulsion of the Government in integrating the tribal
32

33
communities into the mainstream of the society. This is a sociological process, which needs
to be addressed through the process of time only. However, the Committee notes that the
tribes are living amidst reserved forest land. These tribals, may at some point of time in
future come out and mix up with the civilised society. Therefore, some provision has to be
made so that when they enter the civilised world, they should be given an opportunity to
use the forest land and do the farming. While preserving the uniqueness of the tribals, the
process of integration into the mainstream of the society may continue as per requirement
at a particular point of time. (Para 4.3)
Administrative Issues
The Committee feels that the proposal of the Island Administration for creation of
new district and sub-divisions would help in delegation and decentralization of powers
necessary for quick decision-making. The Committee recommends that the demand of the
Administration may be examined on priority. The new District and sub-divisions would help
the local administration in catering to the needs of people, in an efficient manner and in
the quickest possible time. (Para 5.1)
Need for helicopters
The Committee understands the gigantic task of the administration of 572 islands
spread over 800 kms. They need sufficient vehicles for transportation and aerial route is
the only available means for inter-island transportation. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the proposal for acquisition of two helicopters may be approved at the
earliest. This will help the administration in providing necessary help to the people besides
making the helicopters available for inter-island transport on a regular basis. (Para 5.5)
Personnel Administration
The Committee notes the difficulty being faced by the Administration due to shortage
of staff in providing relief and rehabilitation and completion of other ongoing projects. Such
a large number of vacancies for such a small administrative set-up is a matter of concern
particularly when relief and rehabilitation work is to be done on war footing. The
Committee recommends that the Finance Ministry’s blanket ban on recruitment for the UT
should be reconsidered. The Government should also look into the issue of delay in filling
up of vacancies and take steps to expedite the same. (Para 5.7)
Tourism in the Islands
The Committee desires that the objectives set in the Tenth Five-Year Plan such as
ecofriendly and environmentally sustainable tourism, development of new tourism activities/
products and marketing the Islands as eco-tourism destination, etc. should be achieved. The
schemes taken up needed to be implemented on a priority basis for achieving the objectives
as this would generate employment besides strengthening tourism. The Committee also
recommends that 2006-2007 being the terminal year of the Tenth Five-Year Plan, all-out
efforts may be made so that no activity taken up remains incomplete. (Para 6.5)
The Committee desires that the Government should address both the short-term and
medium-term objectives and take necessary steps for taking up and completion of all the
proposals in a definite timeframe. (Para 6.7)
Andaman and Nicobar Islands are the ultimate unexplored destination of India’s
tourism. Once they are open to tourists there is no doubt that the islands would become

34
one of the tourism attractions in the world. Despite having very good tourism potential,
India has not tapped it well. A&N Islands are a good example of this. There are many
countries in the world which thrive on tourism and India is not able to make use of the
potential. The Committee is, however, happy to note that things are moving in the right
direction with the opening up of more islands in A&N Islands. By opening up islands, more
investment will flow in and tourism will develop which ultimately leads to economic growth
of the islands and the country. The Committee desires that the proposal of opening more
islands for tourism may be got cleared from the Cabinet at the earliest. (Para 6.8)
Air connectivity
The vast potential of international tourists can only be tapped if there is world class
airport and other infrastructure. Air connectivity and tourism are inter-linked and inter-
dependent. A&N Islands, being remotely and strategically located, need better air
connectivity both domestic and international for better tourist arrivals. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should take steps to declare Vir Savarkar Airport as an
International Airport as a step towards projecting A&N Islands as an attractive tourist
destination. The Committee also recommends that to begin with the Government can make
the stopover for Chennai-Bangkok and Chennai-Singapore flights at the Islands. It also
urges upon the Administration to complete the expansion work of the airport expeditiously,
thus making it capable for operation of wide-bodied aircraft. The Committee is also of the
view that the other proposals in the strategy for post-tsunami tourism promotion, if
implemented, will go a long way in the promotion and strengthening of tourism in Andaman
and Nicobar Islands, particularly the proposal relating to introduction of flights from various
cities to Port Blair will go a long way in attracting tourists from different destinations of
the country to the Islands. The Committee desires that the above proposals may be taken
up on top priority. (Para 7.3)
AGRICULTURE AND FISHERY
The Committee is of the view that considering the vast potential of fisheries, shrimp,
crab and prawn, concerted efforts need be made to explore the potential by diversifying
fishing to Shrimp, Crab and Prawn culture. The issue of identification of suitable areas for
coastal shrimp culture may be pursued with Central Institute of Brackishwater Aquaculture
(CIBA). This is necessary in view of scarcity of freshwater in the Islands. The Committee
notes that land available in the Islands is very less and its optimum use should be made.
Besides diversifying fanning practices, efforts should also be made to increase productivity.
Efforts being made to utilise vacant hilly land for plantation, spices, crops, etc., may be
intensified as these are eco-friendly and they grow naturally. Similarly, diversification of
agriculture by encouraging plantation of cash crops such as cashew nuts, spices, and coconut
in the Islands might prove to be a panacea for improving the economic condition of the
farmers and the tribals living in the region. (Para 8.4)
STATEHOOD TO PONDICHERRY
The Committee takes note of the views expressed by a section of the society in
Pondicherry and feels that the sentiments of the people and the people’s elected
representatives cannot be ignored. The overwhelming view of all of them is in favour of
Statehood to the Union Territory of Pondicherry with Special Category status. The
Committee feels that the aspirations of the people have to be respected. The Committee
takes due note of the views of the Ministry that it will not be a viable State economically.
But the Committee cannot be oblivious to the fact that when Goa graduated into a State,

35
there were apprehepsions that Goa might not sustain as a State because of its weak
financial base. But, today, Goa has proved it otherwise. Further, Pondicherry has a
Legislative Assembly with elected representatives. (Para 9.7)
The Committee is also given to understand that Pondicherry Government appointed
a Committee to go into its viability as a State and the then Chief Secretary of Pondicherry
had submitted the Report; the Report was examined and it was agreed, in principle, by the
Government that it would bring forward a Bill in the Parliament to grant Special Category
Status to Pondicherry. However, this proposal was shelved. (Para 9.8)
Looking at the practical point of view, the Committee is of the view that
Pondicherry, as a Union Territory, is a big handicap for the Chief Minister to function. Most
of the administrative powers are vested in the Lieutenant-Governor and files are cleared by
him. (Para 9.9)
Taking into account all these factors, the Committee is of the view that the issue
of Statehood to Pondicherry needs to be considered in a holistic manner. The Committee,
therefore recommends that Government may consider. granting Statehood to Pondicherry
with Special Category Status. (Para 9.10)
B-II CATEGORY STATUS TO PONDICHERRY
The city of Pondicherry, which is also the capital of the UT of Pondicherry, has been
undergoing a rapid transformation. It has all the characteristics of a developed urban
agglomeration. The Committee takes note of the fact that the population of urban
agglomeration of Pondicherry exceeded 5.05 lakhs as per the Census of 2001. The rapid
growth of administration, .industrialization, educational institutions; the population of urban
agglomeration exceeding five lakhs; the floating population of about one lakh per day,
justify the grant of B II status to Pondicherry. The Committee is also given to understand
that Port Blair and Panji were granted B II status, even though their population was less
than that of Pondicherry. The Committee expresses its concern over the discriminatory
attitude shown towards Pondicherry. When Port Blair and Panaji have been granted B II
stdus, the Committee cannot buy the argument given by the Government in respect of
Pondicherry. B II status, besides increasing HRA to Government employees will also
enhance the status of the city. The city will be able to get urban development schemes and
more opportunities for development. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that
Government may grant B II status to Pondicherry city for the purpose of payment of HRA.
The Committee urges upon the Government that the relaxation made in the case of the
cities of Port Blair and Goa in this regard may also be extended to Pondicherry so that the
officials of the Central/UT Government are adequately compensated for their expenditure on
housing. (Para 10.3)
RECOGNITION OF SCHEDULED TRIBES IN PONDICHERRY
The Committee expresses its concern that even though the UT Administration of
Pondicherry has been recommending for recognition of the Scheduled Tribes, the
Registrar General of India has not taken any positive decision so far. His views on five
criteria are not pragmatic and hence may be dispensed with. The Committee also notes that
the above mentioned tribes existed in UT of Pondicherry even before its independence in
1954, as per the reports of Backward Classes Commission of Pondicherry. The Committee
is of the view that RGI is procrastinating the matter. Keeping in view the existence of
scheduled Tribes as identified by the Government of Pondicherry, Backward classes
commission and the Ethnographic study of Dr. Subramniyan Naidu, the Committee

36
recommends notification by Government of the five Scheduled Tribes identified by the UT
Administration of Pondiicherry in terms of Articles 342 read with Article 366 (25) of the
Constitution. (Para 11.2.2)
ELECTION TO PANCHA YATI RAJ INSTITUTIONS
The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that in spite of the
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) having been granted constitutional status, and under
Articles 243 (K) and (L) of the Constitution regular elections are required to be held to the
panchayats every five years, elections thereto have not been held in Pondicherry for the
last 30 years. In this connection, the Committee takes notes of the constitutional provision
under Article 243 E (3). The Committee takes strong exception to the non-compliance of the
constitutional obligation. The Committee is happy to learn that the order conducting
elections to Panchayati Raj Institutions has been issued recently. (Para 12.4)
PERSPECTIVE PLAN FOR TOURISM DEVELOPMENT
The Committee feels that in view of the historical significance and geographical
location, Pondicherry has the potential to develop into a good tourist destination. The
Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Pondicherry Government in making
it as an ideal tourist destination. Airports are an important ingredient for growth of tourism
and in that direction the Committee recognizes the necessity of Pondicherry and Karaikal
airports. The Committee recommends that the Central Government should make all efforts
for early operationalisation of the Pondicherry Airport and establishing of Karaikal Airport.
The Committee also recommends that the development of Pondicherry and Karaikal Ports
and Art and Craft Village in Murungapakkam may be taken up and completed at the
earliest as these would give good infrastrucutral support required for tourism. Construction
of Star Hotels may also be taken up and the development of Medical Tourism may be
emphasized. (Para 13.3)
AGRICULTURE AND IRRIGATION
The Committee expresses its concern over the fast declining net area sown and low
agricultural productivity in tbe last ten years. Productivity remaining static, land
degradation, poor soil .management and excessive exploitation of water resources indicate
the poor health of agriculture sector. The proposal of the UT of Pondicherry to open Uzhavar
Udhaviyagams (Farmers’ Help Centres) is a path-breaking solution to the ills ailing the
farm sector. The Committee is happy to learn that the plan has been implemented and feels
that it should be pursued in the right perspective. (Para 14.3)
FISHERY DEVELOPMENT
The Committee is of the view that early action is needed to bring the people
belonging to agricultural and fishermen communities affected by Tsunami, back to
normalcy. Some rehabilitation measures have already been taken. Now, it is time that
sufficient infrastructure is in place so that they could start leading normal life. The
Committee desires that the comprehensive plan for modernizing fishing activities initiated
by the Government may be implemented at the earliest. For promotion of shrimp culture
clearance of Aquaculture Authority may be obtained at the earliest. Identification of
cultivable land may be completed soon so that shrimp culture may be developed at the
earliest. (Para 15.4)

37
Rehabilitation and Reconstruction
The tsunami tidal waves have caused widespread devastation in the islands resulting
in loss of human life as well as livestock besides loss of property. The Committee feels that
considering the magnitude of destruction of life and property, whatever rehabilitation that
has been provided would not match the loss caused by the natural calamity. But the relief
provided will mitigate the suffering though the scares may not be removed permanently.
However, the Government should not leave any stone unturned to ensure early
rehabilitation of the affected people and to undertake reconstruction process to ensure that
they start their normal life at the earliest. The Committee understands that the
Government have taken up several relief measures. In regard to construction of permanent
houses, the Committee feels that the permanent shelters should be at locations which are
high on ground near the earlier habitations as the livelihood of the people requires them
to continue residing there. Similarly, while constructing the houses, use of local material
such as bamboo, wood, etc., should be preferred as they are earthquake-resistant and give
better protection from sun. The Committee also takes note of the fact that some people,
who met the Committee during its visit, desired that money may be provided to their
families so that they can construct their houses themselves. This is a better proposition
because it will engage the families in the reconstruction work till the completion of the
construction. The Government may therefore, consider providing them financial help besides
other required material to enable the families engage themselves in the reconstruction
work. (Para 19)
The Committee has noted that revival package for small traders consists of waiver
of loans and interest thereon, etc. The Committee recommends that the Government may
consider increasing the package of Rs. 57.15 crore further. It also recommends that the
Government may consider providing interest-free fresh loans for at least two years to
enable them to start their business afresh. Though the Government has given compensation
for loss of agricultural crops which is now Rs. 22,231 per hectare, this is a pittance
considering the fact that agricultural land has new become saline and uncultivable and
barren. It can no longer be used for any agricultural activities and even grass will not grow.
Therefore, the Government should consider providing some package for permanent
rehabilibition of the farmers whose agricultural land is no longer useful. The package may
also contain providing assistance for business or employment. (Para 19.1)
The Committee feels that the request of the people in the islands for employment
to at least one person in each affected family needs to be considered. A one-time creation
of employment opportunities would give permanent relief to the families. Besides this,
filling up of 3000 vacant posts would also cover a large number of people. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Government may consider these proposals immediately and
take decisions thereon. (Para 19.2)
Pondicherry
The Committee notes that about 800 hectares of agricultural land as well as crops
were affected by the tidal waves in Pondicherry. Much of the land may remain permanently
unfit for farming. The relief given may not give permanent compensation to the affected
people. In all the cases of permanent loss of land, the Committee suggests that the
Government may consider raising the compensation appropriately. (Para 21)
After tsunami, many farmers have been severely affected with many children
getting orphaned. Though Government has provided relief package and rehabilitation, it
may also consider providing permanent compensation in the form of reservation in

38
employment to such victims. This is all the more necessary in the case of orphaned
children. (Para 21.1)
In regard to construction of permanent houses, the Committee expresses its concern
that out of 10,061 houses, only 341 houses have been completed so far and it feels that this
way it is going to take a long time for completing all the houses. The Committee
recommends that the pace of construction may be increased and all the houses may be
completed within a definite time frame. Land acquisition for construction of houses may be
completed at the earliest so that construction may start at the earliest. (Para 21.2)
The World Bank aided project is an appreciable effort of the international agency.
Government may monitor the project so that targets are achieved within the given time
frame. (Para 21.3)
Legislature for Chandigarh
The Committee notes the view of the Home Secretary that the present arrangement
is working satisfactorily. However, when the Committee visited Chandigarh, various political
leaders and general public informed that there was no forum to ventilate their grievances.
The Committee is also constrained to learn that it is very difficult for the general public
to meet the Administrator and that they felt that the present arrangement is not able to
solve their problems. The Committee is of the view that the Municipal Corporation cannot
solve all the problems of the people and the Advisory Council cannot help things to the
extent people want their aspirations to be fulfilled. Thus, there needs to be some
mechanism by which people have better access to the administration and which can address
and redress their grievances. Such mechanism, besides solving the problems of the people,
would also fulfill their aspirations. Therefore, keeping in view the aspirations of the people’s
representatives and the general public at large, the Committee recommends that some kind
ot arrangement should be put in place in the UT of Chandigarh which should be easily
accessible to the public and which could effectively and adequately redress their grievances.
(Para 23.4)
Metropolitan Planning Committee
The Committee notes that the Metropolitan Planning Committee can go a long way
in solving the problems of the people of Chandigarh and fulfilling their aspirations. Even
though the Metropolitan Planning Committee is not the ultimate solution to the elected
legislative body, it can, to a large extent, address the problems of the masses. The
Committee suggests that suitable legislation may be brought in at the earliest so that steps
may be initiated for setting up of the Metropolitan Planning Committee. (Para 24.2)
Advisory Council to Administrator
The Committee understands that infrequent meetings of the Advisory Council to
Administrator might be causing problems in redressing the grievances of the people. In the
absence of a legislative body, at least, other bodies such as the Advisory Council should be
given the necessary teeth to address the people’s grievances. The Committee agrees with
the Home Secretary that the Council should meet more frequently. The Committee,
therefore, suggests that necessary steps may be taken in that direction to ensure that the
Council meet more frequently. The Committee also agrees with the view of the Home
Secretary that members of the Advisory Council should be adequately empowered. It
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take necessary steps to redefine the
powers and functions of the members of the Advisory Council and steps may also be taken

39
to give more powers to the Council as such. As regards the suggestion of Home Secretary
that the Council needs to be broad-based, the Committee has not received any concrete
proposal from the Ministry. The Committee, however, feels that the issue needs to be
deliberated upon and steps taken in this direction too. (Para 25.3)
Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh
The Committee is constrained to learn from the Mayor and Councillors of Municipal
Corporation of Chandigarh that it has more responsibilities with limited authority and
financial resources. The Committee has noted the MCC’s request for a share of 23 per cent
of the tax revenue. The Committee is of the view that a municipal body functions closest
to the people and needs to solve problems at the quickest possible time. For this purpose,
it requires sufficient resources. The Committee recommends that the Union Ministry of
Home Affairs may discuss the issue with the Mayor and Councillors of MCC on its
requirement of resources for a better upkeep of the city. Steps may be taken for early
implementation of the Second Delhi Finance Commission recommendations for devolution of
17 per cent share of tax revenue until the Third Delhi Finance Commission takes a decision
on the proposed devolution of 23 per cent tax revenue. (Para 26.9)
The Committee understands that the Zila Parishad and the Panchayati Raj Institutions
(PRIs) in 18 villages would come to an end should the jurisdiction of Municipal Corporation
of Chandigarh be extended to these villages. And in the absence of any demand from the 18
villages for extension of jurisdiction of the MCC into their areas and the orientation of MCC
being urban, these villages may lose their rural identity without entailing any benefits and
urban taxation of the municipality may add to their woes. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the rural identity of the 18 villages may not be disturbed. (Para 26.10)
Scheduled Caste Certificates
The Committee is constrained to note that such an important issue has been kept
unresolved for so long and the people belonging to the SC community had to suffer. Such
issues need to be attended to without delay. The Committee trusts that Home Secretary
would stick to the assurance made before the Committee and the issue would be resolved
immediately. (Para 27.4 )
Career prospects and other grievances of Government teachers in the UT
The Committee gathers that the Chandigarh Administration is either ignorant of or
non-responsive to the problems and issues of Government Teachers. Such inept handling of
their problem would demoralise them. The Committee recommends that the problems faced
by the teachers may be addressed properly. (Para 28.1)
Air, Rail and Road Transport for Chandigarh
The Committee recommends that considering the growing importance of the
Chandigarh city, the Government should explore the possibility of upgrading the Civil
Airport to an International Airport and make it twenty-four hours airport. The railway
service may also be further improved keeping in view the requirement of the city and the
region. (Para 29.1)
Building bye-laws
The Committee feels that the situation that has arisen in Chandigarh is more or

40
less similar to the situation that arose in Delhi in the recent past. The Committee takes
note of the serious situation that arose in Delhi when Courts passed orders for demolition/
sealing of unauthorized constructions in Delhi leading to a public outburst as a large
number of buildings/houses were found to be affected by the said drive. Consequently, the
Central Government had to step in to prevent the situation from further worsening and
Parliament enacting a special legislation for the purpose. To avoid such a situation in
Chandigarh where too alteration/additions in houses have been made on a large scale, the
Committee feels that the Government should bring about a practical solution to the problem
by having a re-look at the building bye-laws of Chandigarh, which are quite old and also
keeping in view the needs of expanding families. Government may also in this context
consider giving a one time relaxation to the building bye-laws in Chandigarh. (Para 32)

3.1 Another Member while citing the example of the Mizoram Accord, was of the view that

3.2 Another Member felt that the Government should not allow foreign observers to oversee the
elections in Jammu and Kashmir. He hoped that the elections would bring back normalcy in that

3.3 A Member was of the opinion that since 1998 the issue of Jammu and Kashmir had been

better than the foreign countries. He felt that the Government should have taken advantage of
Shri Jethmalani’s initiative besides making public a policy framework on Jammu and Kashmir.
3.4 A Member felt that there was no need for discussing the issue when the Committee was
not going to make any recommendation to the Government. Besides, he also stated that the Election
Commission was responsible for free and fair elections and it was not right to presume that
without the imposition of the President’s Rule, free and fair elections could not take place.
3.4.1 Responding to the point raised by the Member, the Chairman clarified that it was on the
request of Shri Jethmalani that the discussion on the subject had been included in the Committee’s
agenda. He further clarified that the idea was to hear the presentation of Shri Jethmalani on the

45
